```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "")
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(lme4))

# Formatting helpers for numbers printed in the text.
f <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x, d = 0) {
  paste(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "per cent")
}
nw <- function(n) {
  words <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight",
             "nine", "ten", "eleven", "twelve")
  if (n >= 1 && n <= 12 && n == round(n)) words[n] else
    formatC(n, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
}
Nw <- function(n) tools::toTitleCase(nw(n))
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) <= 1) return(x)
  paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
}
# A share written as a word where one fits.
frac_word <- function(x) {
  words <- c(`0.5` = "half", `0.25` = "a quarter", `0.75` = "three quarters")
  key <- format(x)
  if (key %in% names(words)) words[[key]] else f(x)
}
# Monte Carlo standard error of a proportion estimated from R replicates.
mcse_p <- function(p, reps) sqrt(p * (1 - p) / reps)
```

# Summary {.unnumbered}

theoryforge reads a scientific theory written as a structured file and
computes from it what the stated causal graph implies, how completely the file
states what its checklist asks for and how a later version of the file compares
with an earlier one. Its computations on a given file are correct. What has not
been studied is everything that happens before and after the file: whether
different researchers encode the same verbal theory into files that give the
same results, whether the checklist score agrees with expert judgements of how
completely and how testably a theory is specified, whether the verdicts of
`appraise_amendment()` agree with expert appraisals of the same amendments,
and whether readers take the outputs to mean what they say.

This protocol describes three studies that would decide what can be claimed.
Study 1 measures how reliably trained coders encode published verbal theories,
from the constructs and the elements of the file to the derived implications
and the checklist score, and sets that agreement beside human and agent
baselines. Study 2 compares the checklist and the appraisal with blind expert
ratings and tests whether known groups of corroborated, refuted and
pseudoscientific theories differ as they should. Study 3 is a randomised reader
study that compares the rate at which researchers and editors misread the
score, the gate, the dossier and the appraisal in the wording of version 0.7.0
and of version 0.8.0, and asks whether the 0.8.0 wording keeps misreading below
a stated tolerance. A last section outlines a later cliometric study of
predictive validity. Every number in this document is computed by the R code
it contains, from inputs stated in that code or read from the repository, so
that a change of assumption changes every number that depends on it.

# Background {#sec-background}

## What the package computes and what it does not

```{r}
#| label: inputs-external
# Values reported by published sources, as stated in the place named.
external <- list(
  # Bornmann, Mutz and Daniel (2010), abstract and Table 1: mean reliability
  # between reviewers of the same manuscript on the intraclass correlation
  # scale, from a random-effects model in which product-moment correlations
  # were squared to that scale, and mean Cohen's kappa.
  reviewer_icc = 0.34, reviewer_kappa = 0.17,
  # Hoekstra et al. (2014), abstract: researchers and students endorsed, on
  # average, more than three of six false statements about a confidence
  # interval.
  false_endorsed = 3, false_items = 6,
  # Hale et al. (2020), abstract: theories represented and sent to authors or
  # experts for feedback, and those finalised only after changes to their
  # constructs, relations or both.
  hale_theories = 71, hale_changed = 36,
  # Jüni et al. (1999), abstract: quality scales used to identify
  # high-quality trials in one meta-analysis.
  juni_scales = 25
)
```

theoryforge takes as input a file that lists a theory's constructs,
propositions, predictions, phenomena, rivals, assumptions and test outcomes.
From the file, it derives the conditional independencies and the signs of
effects that the causal graph of the propositions implies, scores the file
against a checklist, compares the theory with rivals and appraises an amended
version against an earlier one by fixed rules that borrow the terms of
@lakatos1970. Checks made before the 0.8.0 release found the deductive
computations correct: they agree with independent implementations on every
file examined. The same checks found three gaps that no computation on a file
can close.

The first gap is encoding. A verbal theory does not determine its file. In an
encoding pilot (@sec-pilot), encoders given the same source texts produced
files that agreed on the plain statements of a theory and differed on what the
texts leave open, and the derived implications followed the files.
@hale2020 report a similar difficulty for a related representation: of
`r external$hale_theories` behaviour change theories represented as
construct-relationship triples, `r external$hale_changed` were finalised only
after changes to their constructs, their relations or both, following feedback
from the theories' authors or other experts. Whatever the package derives is
therefore a property of an encoding. Whether it is also a property of the
theory depends on how much encodings agree, which is unknown for human
encoders.

The second gap is the checklist score. The checklist reads whether fields are
filled in, how predictions are labelled and whether stated claims agree with
the causal graph. Version 0.8.0 calls the result the checklist score and
states that it describes how completely the file states what the checklist
asks for, that no study has established what difference between two scores is
meaningful and that the score does not show that the theory is true or well
reasoned. That statement describes the file correctly. It leaves open whether
the score, or the item statuses behind it, track what methodologists mean by a
completely and testably specified theory. Summary quality scores have a poor
record elsewhere: when @juni1999 used `r external$juni_scales` quality scales
to identify the high-quality trials in one meta-analysis, some scales showed an
effect only in the high-quality trials and others only in the low-quality ones,
and the summary scores were not significantly associated with the estimated
treatment effects. Validity concerns the inferences drawn from scores, and
@messick1995 distinguishes content, substantive, structural, generalisability,
external and consequential aspects of the evidence for them. For this score,
none has been examined.

The third gap is the appraisal. `appraise_amendment()` labels an amendment
progressive, degenerating or neutral by rules applied to what the two files
declare. The rules are explicit and reproducible, but their agreement with the
appraisals that researchers or historians would make of the same episodes
[@lakatos1970; @meehl1990] has never been measured.

Formalising a theory also leaves untouched what Eronen and Bringmann
[-@eronen2021] identify as reasons
why good psychological theories are hard to develop: the lack of robust
phenomena, the doubtful validity of constructs and the difficulty of finding
causal relations. The studies below do not address these. They address whether
the package's own outputs mean what its documentation says they mean. In
Messick's terms, Study 1 bears on the generalisability aspect of validity, here
across encoders, Study 2 on the external aspect and Study 3 on the
consequential aspect.

## The encoding pilot {#sec-pilot}

```{r}
#| label: inputs-pilot
# Encoding pilot: agent encoders of one model family each encoded the same
# verbal theories from summaries of about 600 words, analysed at commit
# f72ce4c. Every value is read from the pilot's tables in data/pilot.
read_pilot <- function(name) {
  read.csv(file.path("data", "pilot", paste0(name, ".csv")),
           check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
# units_agreement: statements segmented from the sources, statements made
# into the same kind of element by every encoder, Fleiss' kappa on the element
# type (fleiss_fine) and on whether the statement carries a machine-readable
# claim (fleiss_claim), and each encoder's codes: P proposition, PRc
# prediction with a claim, PRn prediction without one, PH phenomenon, A
# assumption, B boundary condition, EV evidence, ALT rival, FF only in a
# definition, mechanism or functional form.
units_tab <- read_pilot("units_agreement")
units_all <- units_tab[units_tab$theory == "all", ]
units_th <- units_tab[units_tab$theory != "all", ]
parse_codes <- function(x) {
  kv <- strsplit(strsplit(x, " ", fixed = TRUE)[[1]], "=", fixed = TRUE)
  setNames(as.numeric(vapply(kv, `[`, "", 2)), vapply(kv, `[`, "", 1))
}
code_list <- unlist(unname(lapply(units_all[grep("^codes_", names(units_all))],
                                  parse_codes)))
# checklist_by_encoder: the checklist score of each file.
cl_tab <- read_pilot("checklist_by_encoder")
# implications_agreement and edge_agreement: pairwise Jaccard indices of the
# literal basis sets of implied independencies and of the directed edges over
# all constructs ('all') and over the constructs every encoder used ('common').
impl_tab <- read_pilot("implications_agreement")
edge_tab <- read_pilot("edge_agreement")
edge_dir <- function(scope) {
  e <- edge_tab[edge_tab$level == "directed" & edge_tab$scope == scope, ]
  as.matrix(e[grep("^J_enc", names(e))])
}
# construct_agreement: pairwise Jaccard indices of the matched construct sets,
# and for 'all three' the constructs in every file (n_a) and in any (n_b).
con_tab <- read_pilot("construct_agreement")
con_pairs <- con_tab[con_tab$pair != "all three", ]
con_union <- con_tab$n_b[con_tab$pair == "all three"]
# structure: constructs, propositions and relation types of each file.
str_tab <- read_pilot("structure")
# checklist_item_spread: the three statuses of each item for each theory.
spread_tab <- read_pilot("checklist_item_spread")
item_statuses <- lapply(split(spread_tab$statuses, spread_tab$item),
                        function(s) unlist(strsplit(s, " / ", fixed = TRUE)))
pilot <- list(
  units = units_all$units,
  units_same_element = as.numeric(sub("/.*", "",
                                      units_all$all_three_same_element)),
  kappa_element = units_all$fleiss_fine, kappa_claim = units_all$fleiss_claim,
  kappa_element_by_theory = units_th$fleiss_fine,
  codes = tapply(code_list, names(code_list), sum),
  scores = with(cl_tab, tapply(aggregate, list(theory, encoder), mean)),
  impl_jaccard = as.matrix(impl_tab[grep("^J_literal_basis_", names(impl_tab))]),
  edge_jaccard = edge_dir("all"),
  edge_jaccard_common = edge_dir("common"),
  construct_jaccard = tapply(con_pairs$jaccard, con_pairs$theory, mean),
  construct_union = con_union,
  constructs = str_tab$constructs,
  propositions = str_tab$propositions,
  relation_types = colSums(str_tab[c("increases", "decreases", "causes",
                                     "moderates")]),
  item_cells_same = sum(as.logical(spread_tab$status_agree)),
  item_cells = nrow(spread_tab),
  item_constant = vapply(item_statuses, function(s) length(unique(s)) == 1,
                         logical(1)),
  item_pass_share = vapply(item_statuses, function(s) mean(s == "pass"), 0)
)
n_pilot_enc <- ncol(pilot$scores)
n_pilot_th <- nrow(pilot$scores)
stopifnot(sum(pilot$codes) == n_pilot_enc * pilot$units,
          sum(pilot$relation_types) == sum(pilot$propositions),
          length(pilot$constructs) == length(pilot$scores),
          length(pilot$construct_union) == n_pilot_th)

# One-way analysis of variance of the scores, theories as groups.
oneway <- function(m) {
  k <- ncol(m); n <- nrow(m); gm <- mean(m)
  msb <- k * sum((rowMeans(m) - gm)^2) / (n - 1)
  msw <- sum((m - rowMeans(m))^2) / (n * (k - 1))
  list(icc1 = (msb - msw) / (msb + (k - 1) * msw), msb = msb, msw = msw)
}
pil <- oneway(pilot$scores)
varying_items <- names(pilot$item_constant)[!pilot$item_constant]
```

The pilot asked `r nw(n_pilot_enc)` encoders to encode `r nw(n_pilot_th)` verbal
theories, the Revised Hierarchical Model of bilingual memory [@kroll2010],
collaborative cognitive load theory [@kirschner2018] and habit in health
behaviour [@gardner2015], from summaries of each source. After matching, the
encoders' sets of constructs had a mean pairwise Jaccard index of
`r f(mean(pilot$construct_jaccard))` (from
`r f(min(pilot$construct_jaccard))` to `r f(max(pilot$construct_jaccard))`
over theories). Of the `r pilot$units` statements segmented from the
summaries, `r pilot$units_same_element` became the same kind of element in all
`r nw(n_pilot_enc)` files, with a Fleiss' kappa [@fleiss1971] of
`r f(pilot$kappa_element)`, and agreement on whether a statement carried a
machine-readable claim was lower (kappa `r f(pilot$kappa_claim)`). Literal
agreement on the implied conditional independencies, after matching
constructs, ranged from a Jaccard index of `r f(min(pilot$impl_jaccard))` to
`r f(max(pilot$impl_jaccard))` between pairs of files. The checklist scores of
the `r nw(length(pilot$scores))` files ranged from
`r f(min(pilot$scores), 1)` to `r f(max(pilot$scores), 1)`, and only
`r pct(pil$icc1)` of their variance lay between theories (ICC(1) =
`r f(pil$icc1, 3)`). The files had the same status on
`r pilot$item_cells_same` of `r pilot$item_cells` item-by-theory cells, mostly
because the texts lacked what several items ask for, and
`r nw(sum(pilot$item_constant))` of the `r nw(length(pilot$item_constant))`
items had the same status in all `r nw(length(pilot$scores))` files. Only
`r and_list(paste0("'", varying_items, "'"))` varied.

These values describe agents of one model family that read the same
documentation, working from summaries written by one author, with statements
segmented and constructs matched by one analyst. They say nothing about how
human researchers encode theories, and they offer no standard against which to
judge whether any encoding is faithful. They are used below as one input among
stated alternatives, never as the only basis of a sample size.

## Registration and structure

Each study is described under the headings that a preregistration needs: aims
and hypotheses, design, materials, participants and recruitment, procedure,
measures, analysis plan, sample size, inference criteria and limitations. The
plan of each study will be entered into the PRP-QUANT template of the Joint
Psychological Societies Preregistration Task Force [@bosnjak2022] and
registered before its data collection begins. Studies 1 and 2 share their
sample of theories and their coders and will be registered together. Study 3
is independent of the others and can run first. The analysis scripts will be
registered with the plans, and any deviation will be reported with its reason.

The author of this protocol maintains theoryforge and has an interest in
favourable results. To limit the consequences, the classification of known
groups, the expert ratings and the reader responses are collected by people who
do not see the package's outputs, the confirmatory analyses are run by an
analyst who does not maintain the package, from the registered scripts, on data
whose group labels and conditions are masked until the scripts have been run on
them, and every result is reported whatever its direction.

# Shared materials and methods {#sec-shared}

## Design constants

The constants below fix the design. They are choices, and the sample-size
sections show what follows from them.

```{r}
#| label: inputs-design
design <- list(
  coder_pool = 9,               # trained human coders
  coders_per_theory = 3,        # independent human encodings of each theory
  agent_runs = 3,               # independent agent encodings of each theory
  max_words = 3000,             # longest source passage, figures included
  unitise_check = 0.25,         # share of passages segmented twice
  classifiers = 3,              # panel that assigns the known groups
  hours_per_file = c(low = 4, mid = 6, high = 9),   # coder hours per file
  boot_reps = 2000,             # bootstrap resamples in the analyses
  experts_per_theory = 3,
  expert_pool = 15,
  experts_per_episode = 4,
  rating_scale = c(0, 10),      # expert ratings of each theory
  confidence_scale = c(1, 5),   # expert confidence in a verdict
  hours_per_rating = c(theory = 1, episode = 1.5),  # expert hours
  theories_per_reader = 2,      # Study 3 example theories per participant
  output_types = 4,             # score, gate, dossier, appraisal
  misread_per_type = 4,         # Study 3 statements stating a misreading
  correct_per_type = 4,         # Study 3 statements stating a correct reading
  attention_items = 2,
  alpha = 0.05,                 # two-sided. One-sided tests use alpha / 2.
  power = 0.80,
  halfwidth = 0.10,             # target half-width of agreement coefficients
  rel_halfwidth = 0.25,         # target half-width of the SEM, relative to it
  icc_threshold = 0.50,         # theories account for half the score variance
  agree_level = 0.80,           # agreement at which a file may stand for the theory
  rho_null = 0.30,              # correlation the score must exceed (H2.1)
  rho_true = c(0.5, 0.7),       # true correlations considered for H2.1
  expert_icc_alt = 0.6,         # expert ICC above the reviewer value
  expert_kappa_design = 0.4,    # expert-expert kappa of the design scenario
  expert_kappa_high = 0.6,
  c4_margin = 0.5,              # tolerated shortfall, share of expert agreement
  item_min_share = 0.10,        # least common status needed for item agreement
  misread_tolerance = 0.20,     # tolerated misreading rate in the 0.8.0 arm
  rate_grid = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30),  # true rates considered (H3.2)
  sd_theory_logit = c(0.5, 1),  # Study 1: theory differences in coding accuracy
  sd_coder_logit = 0.3,         # Study 1: coder differences in coding accuracy
  coder_share = 0.25,           # share of encoding variance due to coders
  sd_expert_logit = 0.3,        # Study 2: expert differences in accuracy
  verdict_share = c(progressive = 1, neutral = 1, degenerating = 1) / 3,
  p0_low = 0.25,                # Study 3: lower baseline misreading probability
  or_design = 0.67,             # Study 3: design effect of the 0.8.0 wording
  or_large = 0.5,               # Study 3: larger alternative effect
  p_correct = 0.75,             # Study 3: endorsement of correct statements
  p_correct_alt = 0.9,
  sd_reader = 1.0,              # Study 3: participant SD, logit scale
  sd_item = 0.8,                # Study 3: statement SD, logit scale
  sd_item_slope = 0.3,          # Study 3: SD of the wording effect over statements
  editor_share = 0.25,          # Study 3: share of editors sought
  min_cell = 5,                 # smallest group a deposited combination may describe
  withdraw_months = 1,          # months after data collection until key deletion
  reps_alpha = 500, reps_score = 200, reps_episode = 1000, reps_reader = 150,
  reps_cover = 200, boot_cover = 500,
  n_grid = c(24, 36, 48, 60, 72),      # theories, multiples of the 12 blocks
  ng_grid = 4:100,                     # theories per known group
  ep_grid = c(20, 30, 40, 60, 80),     # amendment episodes
  arm_grid = seq(50, 400, by = 25)     # readers per arm
)
# Derived constants: statement totals, and the non-inferiority margin of
# H3.3, which equals the design effect (see H3.3).
design$misread_items <- design$misread_per_type * design$output_types
design$correct_items <- design$correct_per_type * design$output_types
design$ni_margin_or <- design$or_design
known_groups <- c("corroborated", "refuted", "pseudoscientific")
n_strata <- length(known_groups) + 1
ci_lab <- paste(100 * (1 - design$alpha), "per cent")
z_crit <- qnorm(1 - design$alpha / 2)
```

## Software versions

```{r}
#| label: inputs-repository
# Read from the repository at render time.
checklist <- yaml::read_yaml("../schema/rigor_checklist.yaml")
item_ids <- vapply(checklist$items, function(i) i$id, "")
blockers <- item_ids[vapply(checklist$items,
                            function(i) identical(i$severity_if_fail, "blocker"),
                            logical(1))]
pkg_version <- unname(read.dcf("../r/theoryforge/DESCRIPTION",
                               fields = "Version")[1, 1])
suppressMessages(pkgload::load_all("../r/theoryforge", quiet = TRUE))
example_files <- sort(list.files("../apps/examples", pattern = "[.]theory[.]yaml$",
                                 full.names = TRUE))
example_scores <- vapply(example_files,
                         function(p) tf_check(tf_read(p))$aggregate_score,
                         numeric(1))
names(example_scores) <- sub("[.]theory[.]yaml$", "", basename(example_files))
```

All encodings are run through one release of the package, fixed for the whole
programme and identified in each registration by its commit, version
`r pkg_version` when this document was rendered. The checklist in the
repository at rendering was version `r checklist$schema_version`, with
`r length(item_ids)` items of which `r nw(length(blockers))`
(`r and_list(paste0("'", blockers, "'"))`) can block the gate. Study 3 also
uses the release tagged v0.7.0. Outputs are computed in R and checked in
Python, since the two packages are specified to give the same results.

## Sample of theories {#sec-sample}

Studies 1 and 2 use one sample of published verbal theories in the behavioural
sciences, drawn from three sources. The population the sample represents, and
to which claims C1 to C3 below refer, is published verbal theories of the kind
the first two sources supply.

The first source is the database of behaviour change theories of @hale2020,
which lists theories with their primary sources and gives an independent
representation of each as construct-relationship triples. Theories are drawn
from it at random. The second source is a set of journals that publish
theoretical articles in psychology, searched over a span of years fixed at
registration for articles that propose or revise a named verbal theory. Two
screeners judge eligibility independently, and a third resolves disagreements.
Eligible articles are drawn at random. The third source supplies the known
groups (@sec-known-groups).

A theory is eligible when all of the following hold.

- A primary source by the theory's proponents states it in prose, with at least
  two constructs and at least one stated relation between them.
- The statement can be confined to a passage of at most
  `r f(design$max_words, 0)` words, including its figures and tables, on whose
  boundaries two screeners agree (a third resolves disagreements).
- The source is in English and can be given to every coder and expert.
- The theory has not been stated as a set of equations or as a computational
  model, since the question concerns verbal theories.
- The theory is not one of the pilot theories or the package's shipped
  examples, which serve for training.
- No member of the study team, coder or expert assigned to it is an author of
  the source.

## Known groups {#sec-known-groups}

Groups of `r and_list(known_groups)` theories are added to the sample, with
equal numbers in each (the number is set in @sec-s2-size). With the typical
theories from the first two sources, they form `r nw(n_strata)` strata.

- Corroborated theories are those whose central risky prediction passed tests
  by groups independent of its proponents, documented in a systematic review, a
  multi-laboratory study or a registered replication published before sampling,
  with no unresolved failure of that prediction in tests of comparable quality.
- Refuted theories are those whose central prediction failed in a high-powered
  registered or multi-laboratory test or in a systematic review, and which later
  reviews describe as refuted or as abandoned in its original form.
- Pseudoscientific theories are doctrines presented by their proponents as
  scientific explanations of behaviour, which a scientific body's statement or
  a peer-reviewed review describes as lacking scientific support, and whose
  proponents have met reported failures by changing the doctrine without
  stating new tests or by rejecting the tests. A written statement by the
  proponents of a length comparable with the other sources must exist.

Candidates for each group are listed from structured searches of review
literature, with search strings fixed at registration. A panel of
`r nw(design$classifiers)` methodologists, who are neither coders nor Study 2
experts, assigns each candidate to a group or to none by the criteria above,
independently and before any candidate is encoded. A candidate enters a group
only when a majority of the panel assigns it there, and the panel's agreement
is reported. The classification rests on the empirical and historical record of
each theory and is made without reference to how completely its source
specifies it, so that the groups are not defined by the quantity they are used
to validate. Because the groups were chosen to differ, the analyses that bear
on the population of typical theories are made within strata
(@sec-s1-analysis and @sec-s2-analysis).

## Source passages and statements

For each theory, two screeners fix the passage of the primary source that
states it. Author names, theory names and dates are removed from the passage
where the text allows, and coders and experts receive only this version. A
trained unitiser segments the passage into statements, each stating one
construct, relation, condition, prediction or assumption. A second unitiser
independently segments a random `r pct(design$unitise_check)` of the
passages, and the agreement between the two segmentations is reported. The
coders then work from the segmented passages, so that disagreement about where
a statement begins does not enter the agreement on what it became.

## Written encoding protocol and coder training {#sec-encoding-protocol}

Before Study 1 begins, the encoding protocol will be written down and fixed.
It states conventions for the choices that produced most disagreement in the
pilot. They say

- when a stated relation also becomes a prediction,
- how an interaction is encoded, since encoding it as `moderates` leaves the
  moderated relation unsigned,
- how a feedback loop is encoded,
- that a mechanism field is filled only when the text gives a reason,
- that no bound, measure or rival is written that the text does not state.

For each statement, the coder records which element or elements of the file it
became, using the pilot's categories (proposition, prediction with or without a
machine-readable claim, phenomenon, assumption, boundary condition, evidence,
rival, wording only) and a further category for a statement left out. For the
analysis, each statement has one value, the combination of categories it
became, so that a statement that became both a proposition and a prediction
with a claim falls in a category of its own. In the pilot, each statement
received one category, a proposition that also became a prediction being coded
as the prediction, and the simulations below assume one category per
statement. Combinations would add categories and lower the agreement expected
by chance.

Coders train on the pilot theories. They receive feedback on the format of
their files and on the use of the protocol, and none on content, since feedback
on content would teach them the trainers' readings and raise their agreement
above what independent users of the protocol would reach. A coder is admitted
after completing the training files with full validation passing. The
reliability estimated in Study 1 therefore applies to researchers trained with
a written protocol, which is more than most users of the package receive.

## Construct matching

Comparing two files requires deciding which construct in one corresponds to
which construct in the other. Two adjudicators, who are not coders, match the
constructs of the files of each theory independently, without knowing which
coder produced which file. Their agreement is reported, disagreements are
resolved by discussion, and every analysis that depends on matching is repeated
with each adjudicator's own matching.

## Agent encoders {#sec-agents}

Each theory is also encoded `r nw(design$agent_runs)` times by an agent: a
language model given the source passage, the written encoding protocol and the
package's documentation, with the package available to validate its files. Each
run starts in a fresh session and sees no human encoding and no other run. The
model's identifier and version, the date and the full instructions are fixed at
registration and archived. The pilot's encoders were agents of one model
family, which may share readings that independent humans would not, so
agreement among agent runs is reported separately and is not treated as
exchangeable with agreement among humans.

## Inputs for the sample-size calculations {#sec-inputs}

The sample sizes below are justified by the precision they give and, for the
hypotheses that are tested, by their power [@lakens2022]. Where no closed form
fits the design, the operating characteristics are estimated by simulation with
fixed seeds, and Monte Carlo standard errors are reported [@morris2019]. The
pilot inputs are in @sec-pilot and the external ones in @sec-background. Two
further inputs come from analyses of shipped example files.

```{r}
#| label: inputs-encoding
# Standard deviation of the checklist score of one theory over every
# combination of a set of binary encoding choices that leave its statements
# unchanged, each combination weighted equally, for the shipped panic-network
# v1 and modality-switching files (32 and 16 combinations), and over all
# choices, including one that deletes construct-level boundary conditions (64
# and 32 combinations). From the reanalysis made before the 0.8.0 release,
# measurement-check/own/03_multiverse_reanalysis.txt in the audit directory
# described in the folder's README.
encoding_sd <- list(
  content = c(panic_v1 = 3.32, modality = 3.36),
  all = c(panic_v1 = 4.81, modality = 5.49)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: inputs-derived
sd_theory <- c(
  pilot = sqrt(max(0, (pil$msb - pil$msw) / n_pilot_enc)),
  examples = sd(example_scores),
  pooled = sd(c(rowMeans(pilot$scores), example_scores)))
sem_in <- c(pilot = sqrt(pil$msw),
            content = mean(encoding_sd$content),
            all = mean(encoding_sd$all))
# Variance between the examples left after removing one encoder's residual
# noise, the part of the encoding variance that is not a stable coder effect.
examples_net <- var(example_scores) - (1 - design$coder_share) * sem_in^2
sdd <- function(sem) z_crit * sqrt(2) * sem
sb <- function(icc, k) k * icc / (1 + (k - 1) * icc)
icc_of <- function(sd_t, sem) sd_t^2 / (sd_t^2 + sem^2)
icc_mid <- icc_of(sd_theory[["examples"]], sem_in[["content"]])
units_per_theory <- round(pilot$units / n_pilot_th)
code_share <- pilot$codes / sum(pilot$codes)
# Edges are compared over all pairs of the constructs that any encoder of a
# theory used, so the pairs per file are those of the theory's union.
pairs_union <- choose(pilot$construct_union, 2)
edge_joined <- sum(pilot$propositions) / (n_pilot_enc * sum(pairs_union))
edge_share <- c(none = 1 - edge_joined,
                rep(edge_joined * pilot$relation_types /
                      sum(pilot$relation_types) / 2, each = 2))
edge_units <- round(mean(pairs_union))
impl_sd <- sd(rowMeans(pilot$impl_jaccard))
edge_sd <- sd(rowMeans(pilot$edge_jaccard))
construct_sd <- sd(pilot$construct_jaccard)
edge_common_higher <- if (all(rowMeans(pilot$edge_jaccard_common) >
                              rowMeans(pilot$edge_jaccard))) "every" else "some"
p_hoekstra <- external$false_endorsed / external$false_items
```

The first input that needs comment is the spread of checklist scores between
theories. The pilot's analysis of variance gives a between-theory standard
deviation of `r f(sd_theory[["pilot"]])` points. The
`r nw(length(example_scores))` example theories shipped with the apps, each a
published theory encoded by one person, have scores from
`r f(min(example_scores), 1)` to `r f(max(example_scores), 1)` and a standard
deviation of `r f(sd_theory[["examples"]])` points. That value includes the
person's encoding noise and is therefore an upper value for the spread among
the examples. Pooling the pilot theories' means with the examples gives
`r f(sd_theory[["pooled"]])` points, which mixes encoders as well as theories
and is used as the widest plausible spread.

The second input is the encoding noise. The pilot's within-theory standard
deviation is `r f(sem_in[["pilot"]])` points. The other values come from a
reanalysis of two shipped files, in which each was scored under every
combination of a set of binary encoding choices that leave the theory's
statements unchanged. The standard deviation of the score over those
combinations, each weighted equally, is `r f(sem_in[["content"]])` points on
average, and `r f(sem_in[["all"]])` when a choice that deletes construct-level
boundary conditions is included. A standard deviation over equally weighted
combinations of choices overstates the noise of one encoder who applies the
same conventions throughout, as the written protocol requires. Taken as the
residual noise of the person who encoded the examples (the encoding variance
less the `r pct(design$coder_share)` of it assumed to be a stable difference
between coders, which is constant for one person), the
content-preserving value would leave no variance between the examples, since
their variance of `r f(var(example_scores))` less a residual variance of
`r f((1 - design$coder_share) * sem_in[["content"]]^2)` is negative. The
pilot's within-theory value would leave a between-theory standard deviation of
`r f(sqrt(max(0, examples_net[["pilot"]])))` points.

The design scenario combines the examples' spread,
`r f(sd_theory[["examples"]])`, with the content-preserving noise,
`r f(sem_in[["content"]])`, under which theories would account for
`r pct(icc_mid)` of the variance of a single encoding's score. It is
optimistic about the spread and pessimistic about the noise. The pilot's
between-theory standard deviation, close to zero, is kept throughout as the
scenario in which typical theories hardly differ in their scores, and the
pooled value as the scenario in which they differ most.

The third input is the human baseline. @bornmann2010 found a mean reliability
of `r f(external$reviewer_icc)` on the intraclass correlation scale and a mean
Cohen's kappa of `r f(external$reviewer_kappa)` between journal reviewers
judging the same manuscript. These values concern recommendations on
manuscripts, not encodings of theories, and a kappa depends on how the codings
are distributed over the categories [@feinstein1990]. They are therefore set
beside the results as a description of how far experts judging the same
scientific document agree, and not as thresholds. The reviewer reliability also
serves as the lower value for the agreement of Study 2's experts.

## Rater assignment {#sec-assignment}

```{r}
#| label: coder-design
# Steiner triple system on 9 coders: 12 blocks of 3, every pair of coders
# together in exactly one block. Theories are assigned to blocks at random.
sts9 <- rbind(c(1, 2, 3), c(4, 5, 6), c(7, 8, 9), c(1, 4, 7), c(2, 5, 8),
              c(3, 6, 9), c(1, 5, 9), c(2, 6, 7), c(3, 4, 8), c(1, 6, 8),
              c(2, 4, 9), c(3, 5, 7))
# Balanced incomplete block design on 6 coders: 10 blocks of 3, every pair
# together in exactly two blocks (used only for comparison).
bibd6 <- rbind(c(1, 2, 3), c(1, 2, 4), c(1, 3, 5), c(1, 4, 6), c(1, 5, 6),
               c(2, 3, 6), c(2, 4, 5), c(2, 5, 6), c(3, 4, 5), c(3, 4, 6))
pair_lambda <- function(b) {
  unique(as.vector(table(apply(b, 1, function(r)
    combn(sort(r), 2, paste, collapse = "-")))))
}
stopifnot(max(sts9) == design$coder_pool,
          ncol(sts9) == design$coders_per_theory,
          length(pair_lambda(sts9)) == 1, length(pair_lambda(bibd6)) == 1,
          length(unique(as.vector(table(sts9)))) == 1,
          all(design$n_grid %% nrow(sts9) == 0),
          all(design$n_grid %% n_strata == 0))
# Cyclic assignment of experts: with units and experts in random order, the
# places of successive units are filled from the list of experts in turn, and
# the list is moved on by one position each time it has been used up.
cyclic <- function(n_units, per_unit, pool) {
  s <- seq_len(n_units * per_unit) - 1
  m <- matrix((s + s %/% pool) %% pool + 1, n_units, per_unit, byrow = TRUE)
  stopifnot(all(apply(m, 1, anyDuplicated) == 0))
  m
}
# Share of pairs of experts that rate no unit in common.
pairs_apart <- function(m, pool) {
  pr <- combn(pool, 2)
  mean(apply(pr, 2, function(p) !any(rowSums(m == p[1]) & rowSums(m == p[2]))))
}
```

Each theory is encoded independently by `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` of
`r nw(design$coder_pool)` coders. The assignment follows a Steiner triple
system: the `r nrow(sts9)` triples of coders are used equally often, so that
every coder encodes the same number of theories and every pair of coders shares
the same number of theories (`r nw(pair_lambda(sts9))` in each cycle of
`r nrow(sts9)` theories). Coders are thus crossed with theories in an
incomplete design, for which @tenhove2024 give guidance on choosing and
estimating intraclass correlations. A pool of `r nw(design$coder_pool)` rather
than `r nw(max(bibd6))` coders spreads the work and estimates stable
differences between coders from more coders, and @sec-s1-size shows how much
that changes the precision.

Experts are assigned by a cyclic design. With theories and experts each in a
random order, the places of successive theories are filled from the list of
the `r design$expert_pool` experts in turn, and the list is moved on by one
position each time it has been used up. Amendment episodes are assigned in the
same way. Each expert then rates the same number of theories or episodes or one
more, and the shift brings different experts together, so that any two experts
are connected through a chain of shared theories, although many pairs share
none.
@sec-final-n gives the counts.

# Claims and hypotheses {#sec-claims}

@tbl-claims lists the claims that the studies examine and the result that would
count against each. They are claims that a reader of the documentation could
reasonably take the package to make, including some that version 0.8.0 no
longer makes in so many words, because the outputs invite them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-claims
#| tbl-cap: "Claims examined, the study that examines each and the result that would count against it."
claims <- data.frame(
  Claim = c(
    "C1. A file encodes the theory, so that what the package derives from it belongs to the theory and not to one encoder's choices.",
    "C2. Differences between the checklist scores of two theories of the same kind reflect the theories rather than their encoders.",
    "C3. The checklist score tracks how completely and how testably experts judge a theory to be specified.",
    "C4. The labels progressive, degenerating and neutral correspond to what an expert applying Lakatos's terms would conclude about the same amendment.",
    "C5. In the 0.8.0 wording, readers do not take the score, the gate, the dossier or the appraisal for judgements of truth or quality."),
  Study = c("1", "1", "2", "2", "3"),
  `Counts against it` = c(
    paste0("Agreement among independent human coders on the constructs, the elements or the signed edges that lies reliably below ", f(design$agree_level), " (H1.1 to H1.3)."),
    paste0("A share of score variance due to theories within strata, ICC(A,1), that lies reliably below ", f(design$icc_threshold), " (H1.4)."),
    paste0("A within-strata correlation with expert ratings of completeness that lies reliably below ", f(design$rho_null), ", or a difference between the pseudoscientific group and the others that lies reliably below the smallest detectable difference (H2.1 and H2.2)."),
    "Agreement of the package's verdicts with experts that is reliably lower than the agreement of experts with each other (H2.3).",
    paste0("For any of the four outputs, a rate of endorsing its misreadings in the 0.8.0 wording that lies reliably above ", pct(design$misread_tolerance), " (H3.2).")),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(claims)
```

Each claim is decided by its own rule, stated with the study that examines it,
with three outcomes: supported, contradicted or open. Error rates are
controlled for each claim, since each answers a separate question and is
reported whatever the others show. A one-sided test at level $a$ asks whether
the one-sided $1 - a$ interval excludes the null value, and its $p$ value is
the smallest $a$ at which it does. For a bootstrap interval, this is
$(1 + b)/(B + 1)$, where $b$ of the $B$ bootstrap replicates lie on the null
side of the null value or at it. A claim that needs several conditions is
supported only when each is met at the one-sided level
`r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)`. It is then wrongly supported only if a condition
that does not hold is judged met, which has a probability of at most
`r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)`, so no adjustment is needed. A claim that any one of
several results would contradict is contradicted when the Holm procedure at
level `r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)` rejects at least one of the corresponding null
hypotheses: the $p$ values are ordered from the smallest, the $k$-th smallest
is compared with `r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)` divided by $m + 1 - k$, where $m$
is the number of results, and testing stops at the first that is not below its
threshold. The probability of wrongly contradicting the claim is then at most
`r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)`. Reliably below or above a level, in @tbl-claims,
means a contradiction by this rule. The sample sizes below are computed at the
levels these rules apply.

# Study 1: encoding reliability {#sec-study1}

## Aims and hypotheses

Study 1 estimates how far independent human coders who follow the written
protocol produce the same file from the same verbal theory, at each level at
which the package reads the file: the constructs, the elements each statement
becomes, the signed edges of the causal graph, the predictions with
machine-readable claims, the derived implications and claim verdicts, the
checklist item statuses and the checklist score. It sets this agreement beside
the reviewer baseline, the agreement of Study 2's experts on the same theories
and the agreement of agent encoders. The study is reported following the GRRAS
guidelines [@kottner2011].

The primary hypotheses state the conditions of claims C1 and C2 at the levels
we take them to need. These levels are our conventions, stated in advance, and
other readers may set them elsewhere.

- H1.1: the coders' sets of constructs agree, after matching, with a mean
  pairwise Jaccard index above `r f(design$agree_level)`.
- H1.2: agreement among coders on the element each statement becomes, measured
  by Krippendorff's alpha, exceeds `r f(design$agree_level)`.
- H1.3: agreement among coders on the status of each pair of constructs in the
  causal graph (no edge, or an edge with its direction and sign), over all
  pairs of the constructs that any coder of the theory used, measured by alpha,
  exceeds `r f(design$agree_level)`.
- H1.4: ICC(A,1) of the checklist score within strata, the share of the
  variance of a single encoding's score due to theories of the same kind,
  exceeds `r f(design$icc_threshold)`.

Claim C1 needs H1.1 to H1.3: `r f(design$agree_level)` is the level at which we
take a file to stand for the theory. At an alpha of `r f(design$agree_level)`
on the element types, with the pilot's distribution of types, about
`r pct((1 - design$agree_level) * (1 - sum(code_share^2)))` of pairs of codings
of a statement would disagree. Claim C2 needs H1.4, so that theories of the
same kind account for more than half of the variance of a single encoding's
score. The agreement of journal reviewers (@sec-inputs) is reported beside
these results as a description and is not tested.

## Design

Study 1 is a reliability study in which `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)`
human coders and `r nw(design$agent_runs)` agent runs encode each theory of the
shared sample independently, with coders crossed with theories in the
incomplete design of @sec-assignment. There is no manipulation.

## Materials

The materials are the segmented source passages of the sample of theories
(@sec-sample and @sec-known-groups), the written encoding protocol, the
package's documentation at the fixed release and a spreadsheet in which coders
record, for each statement, the element or elements it became.

## Participants and recruitment

Coders are doctoral students, postdoctoral researchers or research assistants
with training in a behavioural science and in research methods, recruited by
advertisement in the University of Oxford and in partner institutions. They are
paid for their time at the University's rate for research assistance. People
who have contributed to theoryforge, or who have used it before, are not
eligible. The agent encoders are described in @sec-agents.

## Procedure

After training (@sec-encoding-protocol), each coder receives the passages
assigned to them in a random order. A coder works alone, may consult the
package's documentation and the written protocol and may run the package to
validate the file, and may not consult other coders or any other encoding of
the theory. For each passage, the coder writes a theory file, records the
element each statement became, records the time spent and, for each element,
how confident they are that the text supports it. The coder also records
whether they recognised the theory and, if so, what they knew of its standing.
A file is submitted once full validation passes or once the coder has recorded
why it does not.

Questions about the protocol go to a coordinator, who answers by quoting or
pointing to the rule of the written protocol that applies and never comments on
a particular passage, statement or theory. Each answer is dated and sent to all
coders at once, and the questions and answers are archived. The written
protocol is not changed once encoding has begun. When it does not settle a
case, the coder applies the rule they judge closest and records that they did
so, and these cases are counted and reported.

## Measures {#sec-s1-measures}

All outputs are computed with the fixed release from each submitted file.

- The construct set of each file is the set of its constructs after matching.
  Construct sets are compared by the Jaccard index, averaged over the coder
  pairs of a theory and then over theories.
- The element type of each statement is the category of the element or
  elements it became (@sec-encoding-protocol). Agreement on it is measured by
  Krippendorff's alpha for nominal data [@hayes2007] over statements, and by
  Fleiss' kappa for comparison with the pilot.
- The status of each pair of constructs in the causal graph is no edge, an edge
  in either direction with sign increases, decreases or unsigned causes, or a
  moderation. The pairs are those of all the constructs that any coder of the
  theory used, after matching, and a pair involving a construct that a file
  lacks has the status 'no edge' in that file. Agreement is measured by alpha
  over pairs, and by the mean pairwise Jaccard index of the sets of signed
  edges. Restricting the pilot's comparison to the constructs that all encoders
  shared raised the mean Jaccard index for `r edge_common_higher` theory,
  which is why the comparison is made over all constructs.
- The claims stated by each file (cause, effect, kind and sign) are compared by
  the mean pairwise Jaccard index.
- The derived implications are the basis set of implied conditional
  independencies, compared literally by the Jaccard index after matching
  constructs, and the independence model over the constructs that all coders
  of a theory share, compared by alpha over triples (independent or not, given
  each conditioning set), as in the pilot.
- The verdict of `entailments()` on each claim stated in at least two files of a
  theory (entailed, contradicted, left open or not evaluated) is compared by
  alpha, with missing values for files that do not state the claim.
- The status of each checklist item in each file (pass, warn, fail or not
  applicable) is compared by alpha and by Gwet's AC1, which behaves better than
  kappa when one status is far more common than the others
  [@gwet2008; @feinstein1990], and reported with the prevalence of each status
  and the raw agreement. Agreement is computed only for items whose least
  common status occurs in at least `r pct(design$item_min_share)` of files,
  since a coefficient says little when nearly every file has the same status.
  The other items are described by their prevalence alone.
- The checklist score of each file is analysed as a continuous measure.
- The secondary measures are the agreement of the two unitisers, the time per
  file, the share of files that pass full validation, the coders' confidence,
  their recognition of each theory and, for the theories drawn from
  @hale2020, the agreement of each file's construct-relationship pairs with
  that study's representation.

## Analysis plan {#sec-s1-analysis}

Agreement coefficients are computed over all theories, with statements, pairs
or triples as units and coders as raters, and again within the typical stratum.
Krippendorff's alpha accommodates any number of coders and missing values
[@hayes2007]. Because units are nested in theories and coders are crossed with
theories, intervals come from a bootstrap that resamples theories and coders
independently, the pigeonhole bootstrap of @owen2007, with
`r f(design$boot_reps, 0)` resamples. A theory drawn more than once enters as
that many theories. A coder drawn more than once enters each unit once, since
counting the copies separately would pair a coder's codings with themselves and
add agreement that the data do not contain. A resample in which no unit keeps
two codings is drawn again. Jaccard indices are averaged over coder pairs within
a theory and then over theories, with intervals from the same bootstrap.
@sec-s1-size checks the coverage of these intervals by simulation.

The checklist score is analysed with a linear mixed model with fixed effects
for the `r nw(n_strata)` strata and crossed random intercepts for theories and
coders, fitted by restricted maximum likelihood with lme4 [@bates2015]:

$$y_{ij} = \mu_{s(i)} + t_i + c_j + e_{ij}, \quad t_i \sim N(0, \sigma_t^2),
\quad c_j \sim N(0, \sigma_c^2), \quad e_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma_e^2),$$

where $s(i)$ is the stratum of theory $i$. The fixed effects keep the
differences between strata, which were chosen to be large, out of the
between-theory variance, so that the estimates refer to theories of the same
kind. This assumes that theories differ about as much within each stratum, and
the model fitted to the typical stratum alone is reported beside it. Coders are
treated as random, as @tenhove2024 recommend for interrater reliability. From
the variance components, the analysis reports three quantities.

- ICC(A,1) $= \sigma_t^2 / (\sigma_t^2 + \sigma_c^2 + \sigma_e^2)$, in the
  notation of McGraw and Wong [-@mcgraw1996], is the form of the intraclass
  correlation
  [@shrout1979; @mcgraw1996] that counts differences between coders' mean
  scores as error, as it should when readers compare the scores of theories
  encoded by different people.
- The standard error of measurement of a single encoding is
  SEM $= \sqrt{\sigma_c^2 + \sigma_e^2}$.
- The smallest detectable difference between two theories encoded by different
  coders is SDD $= z\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{SEM}$ with $z$ = `r f(z_crit)`.

Intervals for all three come from a parametric bootstrap of the fitted model
with `r f(design$boot_reps, 0)` replicates, and from the pigeonhole bootstrap,
with the rule above, as a check.

The coders' agreement is set beside the reviewer baseline as a description. It
is compared with the agreement of Study 2's experts on the same theories by the
difference between the within-strata ICC of the score across coders and that of
the experts' completeness ratings across experts, and between the alpha of each
item status across coders and the alpha of the experts' judgements of the
corresponding item, for the items that meet the rule of @sec-s1-measures, with
intervals from a bootstrap that resamples theories, coders and experts by the
same rules. Agent encodings are compared with human ones by the difference
between agent-human and human-human agreement on each measure, and agent-agent
agreement is reported separately.

A coder who leaves is replaced, and their unfinished theories are reassigned so
that each theory keeps `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` human encodings. The
mixed model and alpha both use all available encodings and assume that
encodings are missing at random given the theory and the coder. A file that
never passes full validation is analysed as submitted, and the share of such
files is reported. A statement left without a category is coded as left out.

## Sample size {#sec-s1-size}

The number of theories is set by the precision of the agreement coefficients
and of the SEM. Agreement on element types and on edges is simulated by a model
in which each coder reproduces a statement's true category with a probability
that varies between theories and between coders on the logit scale (standard
deviations `r and_list(f(design$sd_theory_logit, 1))` for theories and
`r f(design$sd_coder_logit, 1)` for coders) and otherwise picks a category at
random from the observed distribution. The intercept is calibrated so that the
population value of alpha equals each target: the pilot's kappa on element
types (`r f(pilot$kappa_element)`), its lower kappa on claims
(`r f(pilot$kappa_claim)`) and the level claim C1 needs
(`r f(design$agree_level)`). Element types follow the pilot's distribution with
`r units_per_theory` statements per theory. Edges follow the pilot's
structure: over all pairs of the constructs that any encoder of a theory used,
`r pct(edge_joined)` were joined by a proposition, and each theory contributes
`r edge_units` pairs.

```{r}
#| label: functions-agreement
# Gauss-Hermite nodes and weights for a standard normal (Golub-Welsch).
gh_nodes <- function(n = 40) {
  i <- seq_len(n - 1)
  J <- matrix(0, n, n)
  J[cbind(i, i + 1)] <- sqrt(i)
  J[cbind(i + 1, i)] <- sqrt(i)
  e <- eigen(J, symmetric = TRUE)
  list(x = e$values, w = e$vectors[1, ]^2)
}
GH <- gh_nodes()
# With accuracy q and errors drawn from the category distribution, two coders
# agree beyond chance by q * q', so the population alpha is E[q q'] for two
# coders of the same theory.
pop_alpha <- function(eta, sd_t, sd_c) {
  inner <- vapply(GH$x * sd_t,
                  function(b) sum(GH$w * plogis(eta + b + GH$x * sd_c)), 0)
  sum(GH$w * inner^2)
}
calibrate_eta <- function(target, sd_t, sd_c) {
  uniroot(function(e) pop_alpha(e, sd_t, sd_c) - target, c(-8, 12))$root
}
# Krippendorff's alpha, nominal, with NA where a coder did not code a unit.
# Units with fewer than two codings are not pairable and are left out.
alpha_nominal <- function(codes, ncat) {
  ok <- !is.na(codes)
  m <- rowSums(ok)
  keep <- m >= 2
  codes <- codes[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  ok <- ok[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  m <- m[keep]
  agree <- numeric(nrow(codes))
  for (a in 1:(ncol(codes) - 1)) for (b in (a + 1):ncol(codes)) {
    agree <- agree + (ok[, a] & ok[, b] & codes[, a] == codes[, b])
  }
  n <- sum(m)
  d_obs <- 1 - sum(2 * agree / (m - 1)) / n
  nc <- tabulate(codes[ok], ncat)
  d_exp <- 1 - sum(nc * (nc - 1)) / (n * (n - 1))
  1 - d_obs / d_exp
}
# One simulated data set: codes (units by coder slots), the coder in each
# slot and the theory of each unit.
gen_codes <- function(n_t, units, share, eta, sd_t, sd_c, blocks) {
  ncat <- length(share); K <- max(blocks)
  assign <- blocks[rep_len(seq_len(nrow(blocks)), n_t), , drop = FALSE]
  theory <- rep(seq_len(n_t), each = units)
  coder <- assign[theory, , drop = FALSE]
  b <- rnorm(n_t, 0, sd_t)
  d <- rnorm(K, 0, sd_c)
  truth <- sample.int(ncat, n_t * units, TRUE, share)
  codes <- vapply(seq_len(ncol(blocks)), function(k) {
    q <- plogis(eta + b[theory] + d[coder[, k]])
    ifelse(runif(length(q)) < q, truth,
           sample.int(ncat, length(q), TRUE, share))
  }, integer(n_t * units))
  list(codes = codes, coder = coder, theory = theory)
}
sim_alpha <- function(n_t, units, share, target, sd_t, sd_c, blocks, reps) {
  eta <- calibrate_eta(target, sd_t, sd_c)
  est <- replicate(reps, {
    g <- gen_codes(n_t, units, share, eta, sd_t, sd_c, blocks)
    alpha_nominal(g$codes, length(share))
  })
  c(mean = mean(est), sd = sd(est))
}
# Pigeonhole bootstrap of alpha: theories and coders resampled independently,
# a coder drawn more than once entering each unit once. Resamples with no
# pairable unit are dropped, which is the same as drawing them again.
pigeonhole_alpha <- function(g, ncat, B) {
  n_t <- max(g$theory); K <- max(g$coder)
  rows_of <- split(seq_along(g$theory), g$theory)
  bt <- replicate(B, {
    rows <- unlist(rows_of[sample.int(n_t, n_t, TRUE)], use.names = FALSE)
    drawn <- unique(sample.int(K, K, TRUE))
    x <- g$codes[rows, , drop = FALSE]
    x[!(g$coder[rows, ] %in% drawn)] <- NA
    alpha_nominal(x, ncat)
  })
  bt[is.finite(bt)]
}
cover_alpha <- function(n_t, units, share, target, sd_t, sd_c, blocks, reps, B) {
  eta <- calibrate_eta(target, sd_t, sd_c)
  res <- t(replicate(reps, {
    g <- gen_codes(n_t, units, share, eta, sd_t, sd_c, blocks)
    bt <- pigeonhole_alpha(g, length(share), B)
    q <- quantile(bt, c(design$alpha / 2, 1 - design$alpha / 2))
    c(est = alpha_nominal(g$codes, length(share)), lo = q[[1]], hi = q[[2]],
      sd_boot = sd(bt))
  }))
  cover <- mean(res[, "lo"] <= target & target <= res[, "hi"])
  c(n = n_t, cover = cover, mcse = mcse_p(cover, reps),
    sd_est = sd(res[, "est"]), sd_boot = mean(res[, "sd_boot"]))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-agreement
set.seed(20261125)
# Sampling noise of one theory's coefficient in the pilot's setting: one
# theory, its statements, three encoders with equal accuracy.
pilot_noise <- sim_alpha(1, units_per_theory, code_share, pilot$kappa_element,
                         0, 0, matrix(seq_len(n_pilot_enc), nrow = 1),
                         design$reps_alpha)[["sd"]]
grid_a <- expand.grid(n = design$n_grid,
                      target = c(pilot$kappa_claim, pilot$kappa_element,
                                 design$agree_level),
                      sd_t = design$sd_theory_logit,
                      kind = c("element", "edge"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
res_a <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(grid_a)), function(i) {
  g <- grid_a[i, ]
  if (g$kind == "element") {
    sim_alpha(g$n, units_per_theory, code_share, g$target, g$sd_t,
              design$sd_coder_logit, sts9, design$reps_alpha)
  } else {
    sim_alpha(g$n, edge_units, edge_share, g$target, g$sd_t,
              design$sd_coder_logit, sts9, design$reps_alpha)
  }
}, numeric(2)))
grid_a$mean <- res_a[, "mean"]
grid_a$sd <- res_a[, "sd"]
grid_a$halfwidth <- z_crit * grid_a$sd
# Monte Carlo standard error of a standard deviation estimated from R replicates.
grid_a$mcse_hw <- z_crit * grid_a$sd / sqrt(2 * (design$reps_alpha - 1))
ok_a <- with(grid_a, aggregate(halfwidth <= design$halfwidth,
                               list(n = n, kind = kind, sd_t = sd_t), all))
first_ok <- function(kind) {
  n_ok <- ok_a$n[ok_a$kind == kind & ok_a$sd_t == min(design$sd_theory_logit) &
                   ok_a$x]
  if (length(n_ok)) min(n_ok) else max(design$n_grid)
}
n_alpha <- first_ok("element")
n_alpha_edge <- first_ok("edge")
```

The pilot's per-theory kappas had a standard deviation of
`r f(sd(pilot$kappa_element_by_theory), 3)`. Sampling alone would give about
`r f(pilot_noise, 3)` for one theory of `r units_per_theory` statements coded
by `r nw(n_pilot_enc)` equally accurate encoders, so the pilot shows
`r if (sd(pilot$kappa_element_by_theory) <= pilot_noise) "no" else "some"`
difference between theories beyond noise, and the theory standard deviations
assumed here allow for more than the pilot shows, as a more varied sample would
need.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-alpha
#| tbl-cap: "Expected half-width of the interval for alpha, the critical value times the standard deviation of the estimates over replicates, by number of theories, target alpha and theory standard deviation on the logit scale."
tab_a <- reshape(grid_a[, c("kind", "sd_t", "target", "n", "halfwidth")],
                 idvar = c("kind", "sd_t", "target"), timevar = "n",
                 direction = "wide")
names(tab_a) <- c("Units", "Theory SD", "Target alpha",
                  paste(design$n_grid, "theories"))
tab_a[, -(1:3)] <- lapply(tab_a[, -(1:3)], f, d = 3)
tab_a$`Target alpha` <- f(tab_a$`Target alpha`)
knitr::kable(tab_a, row.names = FALSE)
```

With `r nw(design$coder_pool)` coders, the coder effects do not average out as
theories are added, so the half-width falls more slowly than the inverse square
root of the number of theories. Under the smaller theory standard deviation,
the half-width of alpha is at most `r f(design$halfwidth)` at every target with
`r n_alpha` theories for element types and with `r n_alpha_edge` theories for
edges. The Monte Carlo standard errors of the half-widths are at most
`r f(max(grid_a$mcse_hw), 4)`.

```{r}
#| label: sim-coverage
set.seed(20261130)
cover_n <- range(design$n_grid)
cover <- t(vapply(cover_n, function(n) {
  cover_alpha(n, units_per_theory, code_share, pilot$kappa_element,
              min(design$sd_theory_logit), design$sd_coder_logit, sts9,
              design$reps_cover, design$boot_cover)
}, numeric(5)))
```

The bootstrap intervals of @sec-s1-analysis were checked on
`r design$reps_cover` simulated data sets of element types at the pilot's kappa
and the smaller theory standard deviation, each resampled
`r design$boot_cover` times. The `r ci_lab` percentile intervals covered the
population value of alpha in `r pct(cover[1, "cover"])` of data sets with
`r cover[1, "n"]` theories and in `r pct(cover[2, "cover"])` with
`r cover[2, "n"]` (Monte Carlo standard errors
`r f(cover[1, "mcse"], 3)` and `r f(cover[2, "mcse"], 3)`). The bootstrap
standard deviation averaged `r f(cover[1, "sd_boot"], 3)` and
`r f(cover[2, "sd_boot"], 3)`, against `r f(cover[1, "sd_est"], 3)` and
`r f(cover[2, "sd_est"], 3)` for the estimates themselves, so the intervals
are, if anything, conservative.

The Jaccard indices have no chance correction and are summarised by their mean
over theories, whose standard error is dominated by differences between
theories. Here, a closed form fits: with a between-theory standard deviation
$s$, a half-width $h$ needs $n = (z\,s/h)^2$ theories. The pilot gives
$s$ = `r f(construct_sd, 3)` for the construct sets, `r f(edge_sd, 3)` for the
signed edges and `r f(impl_sd, 3)` for the implied independencies. Half and
one and a half times the implications value are used as alternatives.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-jaccard
#| tbl-cap: "Theories needed for a given half-width h of the mean Jaccard index, by between-theory standard deviation."
n_jacc <- function(s, h) ceiling((z_crit * s / h)^2)
s_alt <- c(`pilot, construct sets` = construct_sd,
           `pilot, signed edges` = edge_sd, `pilot, implications` = impl_sd,
           `half the implications value` = impl_sd / 2,
           `one and a half times it` = 1.5 * impl_sd)
h_alt <- c(design$halfwidth / 2, design$halfwidth)
tab_j <- data.frame(names(s_alt), f(s_alt, 3),
                    vapply(h_alt, function(h) n_jacc(s_alt, h),
                           numeric(length(s_alt))))
names(tab_j) <- c("Standard deviation", "s", paste("h =", f(h_alt)))
knitr::kable(tab_j, row.names = FALSE)
n_construct <- n_jacc(construct_sd, design$halfwidth)
n_impl <- n_jacc(impl_sd, design$halfwidth)
```

The checklist score is simulated from the mixed model of @sec-s1-analysis in
the incomplete design, with theories spread evenly over the
`r nw(n_strata)` strata and no differences between strata, for every
combination of the three between-theory standard deviations and the three
encoding standard deviations of @sec-inputs, with `r pct(design$coder_share)`
of the encoding variance due to stable differences between coders. Each
replicate is analysed as the real data will be, by restricted maximum
likelihood with the stratum as a fixed effect, and the distribution of the
estimates over `r design$reps_score` replicates gives the precision. Fits that
raise a warning or end on the boundary of the parameter space (a variance
component estimated as zero, which lme4 calls a singular fit) are kept and
counted.

```{r}
#| label: functions-score
ctrl <- lmerControl(check.conv.singular = .makeCC(action = "ignore", tol = 1e-4))
sim_score <- function(n_t, sd_t, sem, coder_share, blocks, reps) {
  K <- max(blocks)
  assign <- blocks[rep_len(seq_len(nrow(blocks)), n_t), , drop = FALSE]
  d <- data.frame(theory = factor(rep(seq_len(n_t), each = ncol(blocks))),
                  coder = factor(as.vector(t(assign)), levels = seq_len(K)))
  d$stratum <- factor(rep_len(seq_len(n_strata), n_t))[d$theory]
  sd_c <- sqrt(coder_share) * sem
  sd_e <- sqrt(1 - coder_share) * sem
  gen <- function() {
    rnorm(n_t, 0, sd_t)[d$theory] + rnorm(K, 0, sd_c)[d$coder] +
      rnorm(nrow(d), 0, sd_e)
  }
  # The template fit, whose estimates are the starting values of every refit,
  # uses unit variance components so that it does not start on the boundary.
  d$y <- rnorm(n_t)[d$theory] + rnorm(K)[d$coder] + rnorm(nrow(d))
  fit <- lmer(y ~ stratum + (1 | theory) + (1 | coder), data = d,
              REML = TRUE, control = ctrl)
  est <- t(replicate(reps, {
    warned <- FALSE
    f_r <- withCallingHandlers(refit(fit, gen()), warning = function(w) {
      warned <<- TRUE
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    })
    v <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(f_r))
    v <- setNames(v$vcov, v$grp)
    c(icc = unname(v["theory"] / sum(v)),
      sem = unname(sqrt(v["coder"] + v["Residual"])), warned = warned,
      singular = isSingular(f_r, tol = 1e-4))
  }))
  icc_sd <- sd(est[, "icc"])
  c(n = n_t, true_icc = icc_of(sd_t, sem),
    icc_mean = mean(est[, "icc"]), icc_sd = icc_sd,
    icc_lo = unname(quantile(est[, "icc"], design$alpha / 2)),
    icc_hi = unname(quantile(est[, "icc"], 1 - design$alpha / 2)),
    sem_mean = mean(est[, "sem"]), sem_sd = sd(est[, "sem"]),
    sem_rel_hw = z_crit * sd(est[, "sem"]) / sem,
    p_half = mean(est[, "icc"] - z_crit * icc_sd > design$icc_threshold),
    warned = sum(est[, "warned"]), singular = sum(est[, "singular"]))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-score
set.seed(20261126)
grid_s <- expand.grid(n = design$n_grid, sd_t = names(sd_theory),
                      sem = names(sem_in), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
res_s <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(grid_s)), function(i) {
  g <- grid_s[i, ]
  sim_score(g$n, sd_theory[[g$sd_t]], sem_in[[g$sem]], design$coder_share,
            sts9, design$reps_score)
}, numeric(12)))
grid_s <- cbind(grid_s, res_s[, -1])
mid <- grid_s$sd_t == "examples" & grid_s$sem == "content"
n_sem_ok <- grid_s$n[mid & grid_s$sem_rel_hw <= design$rel_halfwidth]
n_sem <- if (length(n_sem_ok)) min(n_sem_ok) else max(design$n_grid)
# The smaller coder pool, for comparison, at the largest number in the grid
# that both designs' block counts divide.
n_cmp <- max(design$n_grid[design$n_grid %% nrow(bibd6) == 0])
cmp <- rbind(
  nine = unlist(grid_s[mid & grid_s$n == n_cmp, c("icc_sd", "sem_rel_hw")]),
  six = sim_score(n_cmp, sd_theory[["examples"]], sem_in[["content"]],
                  design$coder_share, bibd6,
                  design$reps_score)[c("icc_sd", "sem_rel_hw")])
# Monte Carlo standard error of the difference between two such SDs.
cmp_mcse <- sqrt(sum(cmp[, "icc_sd"]^2 / (2 * (design$reps_score - 1))))
sing_pilot <- sum(grid_s$singular[grid_s$sd_t == "pilot"]) / sum(grid_s$singular)
pool_sentence <- if (abs(cmp["nine", "icc_sd"] - cmp["six", "icc_sd"]) <
                     2 * cmp_mcse) {
  paste("The difference in the ICC is within twice its Monte Carlo standard",
        "error, so under this scenario the larger pool serves mainly to spread",
        "the work and to estimate coder differences from more coders, which",
        "would matter more if they were larger than assumed.")
} else {
  paste("The larger pool estimates coder differences from more coders, which",
        "narrows the interval.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-score
#| tbl-cap: "Simulated estimation of the checklist score's reliability within strata. True ICC is the share of variance due to theories. The range column holds the central estimates at the interval's level. The SEM half-width is relative to the true SEM. P(> one half) is the approximate probability that the lower interval limit exceeds one half (H1.4). The last column counts singular fits."
tab_s <- data.frame(
  `Theory SD` = paste0(grid_s$sd_t, " (", f(sd_theory[grid_s$sd_t]), ")"),
  `Encoding SD` = paste0(grid_s$sem, " (", f(sem_in[grid_s$sem]), ")"),
  Theories = grid_s$n, `True ICC` = f(grid_s$true_icc),
  `ICC SD` = f(grid_s$icc_sd, 3),
  `Range of estimates` = paste(f(grid_s$icc_lo), "to", f(grid_s$icc_hi)),
  `SEM half-width` = f(grid_s$sem_rel_hw),
  `P(> one half)` = f(grid_s$p_half),
  `Singular fits` = grid_s$singular, check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab_s, row.names = FALSE)
```

Three things follow from @tbl-score. First, the reliability of the score depends
mostly on how much theories of the same kind differ, which no sample size can
change. If published verbal theories differ as little as the pilot theories,
the score's ICC will be low whatever the number of coders, and the study will
show that. Second, under the design scenario, the SEM is estimated within
`r pct(design$rel_halfwidth)` of its value with `r n_sem` theories. Third, at
`r n_cmp` theories under the design scenario, the standard deviation of the ICC
estimate is `r f(cmp["nine", "icc_sd"], 3)` with `r nw(design$coder_pool)`
coders and `r f(cmp["six", "icc_sd"], 3)` with `r nw(max(bibd6))`, and the
relative half-width of the SEM is `r f(cmp["nine", "sem_rel_hw"])` against
`r f(cmp["six", "sem_rel_hw"])`. `r pool_sentence` The probabilities in the
last but one column treat the replication standard deviation as a known
standard error and are approximate, with Monte Carlo standard errors of at most
`r f(max(mcse_p(grid_s$p_half, design$reps_score)), 3)`. Of the
`r f(nrow(grid_s) * design$reps_score, 0)` simulated fits,
`r sum(grid_s$warned)` raised a warning and `r f(sum(grid_s$singular), 0)`
were singular, `r pct(sing_pilot)` of them under the pilot's spread, where the
true ICC is at most `r f(max(grid_s$true_icc[grid_s$sd_t == "pilot"]))`.

```{r}
#| label: n-study1
round_up <- function(x, k) k * ceiling(x / k)
n_study1 <- round_up(max(n_alpha, n_alpha_edge, n_sem, n_construct, n_impl),
                     nrow(sts9))
```

Study 1 needs the largest of the numbers of theories required for alpha on
element types (`r n_alpha`) and on edges (`r n_alpha_edge`), for the SEM
(`r n_sem`) and for the mean Jaccard indices of the construct sets
(`r n_construct`) and the implications (`r n_impl`), rounded up to a multiple
of the `r nrow(sts9)` blocks of the coder design, which is `r n_study1`.
Study 2 may need more, and the final number is set in @sec-final-n.

## Inference criteria {#sec-s1-inference}

Each coefficient is reported with its `r ci_lab` interval, over all theories
and within the typical stratum, and read by the rules of @sec-claims. For each
of the construct sets, the element types and the signed edges, a lower limit at
or above `r f(design$agree_level)` meets a condition of C1 (H1.1 to H1.3). C1
is supported if all three conditions are met, contradicted if the Holm
procedure across the three finds at least one coefficient below
`r f(design$agree_level)`, and otherwise open. C2 is supported if the lower
limit of the within-strata ICC(A,1) exceeds `r f(design$icc_threshold)`
(H1.4), contradicted if the upper limit lies below it, and otherwise open. The
SDD is reported with its interval as the smallest difference between two
theories' scores that the data allow a reader to interpret. If C1 is
contradicted, the documentation must present every derived output as a
property of one encoding, and if C2 is contradicted, it must advise against
comparing the scores of theories encoded by different people.

## Limitations

The theories are a sample of verbal theories in the behavioural sciences, and
the estimates may not transfer to other fields or to theories stated formally.
The ICC is a property of the sample as well as of the procedure, so the SEM and
the SDD, which do not depend on how much the sampled theories differ, are the
more transferable results. The within-strata estimates assume that theories
differ about as much within each stratum, which the typical stratum's own
estimate allows a reader to check. Coders follow a written protocol and receive
training, so agreement among untrained users is likely to be lower. Matching
constructs and segmenting statements are judgements, and their own agreement
limits what the coefficients can show. Agreement is not accuracy: coders could
agree on a reading the theory's authors would reject, which only the
comparison with @hale2020 for a subset, and Study 2, address. Agent encoders
change quickly, so their results describe one model at one date.

# Study 2: criterion and known-groups validity {#sec-study2}

## Aims and hypotheses

Study 2 asks whether the checklist and the appraisal agree with experts who
judge the same theories and amendments without seeing the package's outputs.
Part A concerns theories: the checklist score, the item statuses and a revised
profile are compared with blind expert ratings of how completely and how
testably each theory is specified, and the scores of known groups are
compared. Part B concerns amendment episodes: the verdicts of
`appraise_amendment()` are compared with blind expert appraisals.

The primary hypotheses are:

- H2.1: within strata, the correlation between a theory's checklist score (the
  mean over its `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` encodings) and the experts'
  mean rating of how completely it is specified exceeds
  `r f(design$rho_null)`. A positive correlation is not enough for claim C3:
  even a correlation of `r f(design$rho_null)` would leave
  `r pct(1 - design$rho_null^2)` of the variance of the expert rating
  unexplained.
- H2.2: pseudoscientific theories have lower checklist scores than corroborated
  and refuted theories taken together. A refuted theory was testable enough to
  be refuted, so both scientific groups are expected to score higher than
  doctrines whose proponents avoid tests. If the pseudoscientific group scores
  no lower, the items that read testability do not track it even coarsely.
- H2.3: the agreement of `appraise_amendment()` verdicts with individual
  experts is lower than the agreement of experts with each other. The test is
  framed so that it can count against claim C4: rejecting its null hypothesis
  means the rules agree with experts reliably less well than experts agree
  among themselves. C4 is supported if the lower limit of the difference lies
  above minus `r frac_word(design$c4_margin)` the expert-expert agreement, that
  is, if any shortfall is reliably smaller than
  `r frac_word(design$c4_margin)` of the experts' own agreement.

No hypothesis is made about corroborated against refuted theories. The 0.8.0
documentation says that the score does not show that a theory is true, and a
better specified theory may be easier to refute as well as easier to
corroborate. The difference is estimated with its interval and reported as a
description, without a test (@sec-s2-size gives the reason).

The secondary questions are these.

- How well does each item status agree with the experts' judgement of the
  corresponding item, for the items that meet the rule of @sec-s1-measures?
- Do items whose credit the package checks (against the graph, numeric bounds
  or the lexical screen) agree with experts better than items credited from a
  label or a filled field?
- Does the revised profile agree with experts better than the item statuses?
- How does the score correlate with expert-rated testability and with
  expert-rated empirical standing? The second correlation should be lower than
  the correlation with completeness if the score indexes specification rather
  than standing.
- Do the experts' testability ratings separate the known groups? This checks
  the classification.

## Design

Part A is a correlational validation study with known groups, in which every
theory of the shared sample is rated by `r nw(design$experts_per_theory)`
experts from a pool of `r design$expert_pool`, assigned by the cyclic design of
@sec-assignment. Part B is an agreement study in which each amendment episode
is encoded by `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` coders, assigned as in Study 1,
and appraised by `r nw(design$experts_per_episode)` experts, assigned by the
cyclic design.

## Materials

Part A uses the segmented source passages of Study 1, with author names, theory
names and dates removed where the text allows. For each theory, the experts
answer one question for each checklist item that a passage allows them to
judge, phrased about the theory rather than the file so that 'yes' corresponds
to a pass (@tbl-expert-items), with the answers 'yes', 'partly', 'no' and
'cannot tell'. They give three ratings from `r design$rating_scale[1]` to
`r design$rating_scale[2]`: how completely the theory is specified, how
testable it is as stated and how well supported it is by evidence. They also
say whether they knew the theory before.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-expert-items
#| tbl-cap: "Questions the experts answer about each theory, matched to the checklist items read from the repository. A 'yes' corresponds to a pass."
questions <- c(
  falsifiability = "Does the passage state at least one prediction that rules out some possible result?",
  precision = "Does it state the size or the range of an expected value or effect?",
  risk_severity = "Do its predictions forbid a large part of the results that were possible before the study?",
  non_redundancy = "Can each of its constructs be told apart from the others by its definition?",
  construct_clarity = "Is each construct defined, with how it is measured and where it applies?",
  scope = "Does it state the conditions under which it applies?",
  logical_why = "Does each stated relation come with a reason or a mechanism?",
  causal_testability = "Does it state at least one causal relation?",
  diagnosticity = "Does it name a rival account and a result that would favour one over the other?",
  derivation_chain = "Do its predictions follow from its stated relations?")
# Items without a question (the text below gives the reasons).
excluded_items <- c("parsimony", "formalisation")
stopifnot(setequal(c(names(questions), excluded_items), item_ids))
q_items <- item_ids[item_ids %in% names(questions)]
knitr::kable(data.frame(Item = q_items, Question = unname(questions[q_items])),
             row.names = FALSE)
parsimony_na <- mean(item_statuses[["parsimony"]] == "n/a")
```

`r Nw(length(excluded_items))` items have no question. The item 'parsimony'
applies only to an assumption added for a failed prediction, which a single
