passage does not record. Its status was 'not applicable' in
`r if (parsimony_na == 1) "all" else pct(parsimony_na)` of the
`r nw(length(pilot$scores))` pilot files, and an expert could not judge it
without the theory's later history. The item 'formalisation' credits a declared
formal model, which the eligibility rules exclude, so it is constant by design
for the package and the experts alike. Both are left out of the item-level
comparisons.

Part B uses documented amendment episodes. An episode is eligible when a
published theory (the prior version) was revised in a later publication by
members of the same research programme (the amended version), when the later
publication states that the revision responds to at least one stated empirical
result, when that result is reported in a source published between the two
versions, and when both versions can be confined to passages that meet the
criteria of @sec-sample. Episodes are found by a search, fixed at registration,
for articles whose title or abstract presents a revised, extended or updated
version of a named theory in the behavioural sciences, and by a search for
published case studies that appraise an amendment in Lakatos's terms. Eligible
episodes are drawn at random. Experts receive the two passages and the report
of the result, with names and dates removed where possible, and a one-page
summary of the concepts of progressive and degenerating problemshifts written
from @lakatos1970 without reference to the package's rules. For each episode,
they give a verdict (progressive, neutral or degenerating), their confidence
from `r design$confidence_scale[1]` to `r design$confidence_scale[2]`, the
reasons for the verdict and whether they recognise the episode.

The revised profile is the item-wise report in which each item's credit is
marked as checked by the package, declared by the author or not assessed, with
counts. Its definition will be fixed as code, registered with the analysis
scripts and applied to the files before any expert rating is unmasked.

## Participants and recruitment

Experts are researchers with a doctorate and publications either in the area of
the theories they rate or in research methods or the philosophy of science.
They are recruited through professional networks, the mailing lists of learned
societies and invitations to authors of methodological reviews, and receive an
honorarium. Experts do not take part as coders, classifiers or Study 3
participants, and none rates a theory or episode of which they are an author.
Amendment episodes are encoded by the Study 1 coders, under the same protocol
and the same assignment design, with each file recording the test outcomes that
the sources report as of the amended version.

## Procedure

Experts work online, alone and at their own pace. Each receives the passages
assigned to them in a random order, answers the item questions and the ratings
for each theory, and appraises the episodes assigned to them. They never see a
theory file, a package output, a group label or another expert's ratings. The
package's outputs are computed by the analyst from the coders' files and are
not joined to the expert data until the analysis scripts have been registered
and run on data with the group labels masked.

## Measures

- From the package, for each file: the checklist score, the status of each
  item and the revised profile.
- From the package, for each episode and coder: the verdict of
  `appraise_amendment()` on the coder's prior and amended files, with the other
  keys it reports.
- From the experts: the item answers, the three ratings and prior knowledge of
  each theory, and for each episode the verdict, confidence, reasons and
  recognition.
- From the coders: whether they recognised each theory (Study 1).
- From the classification panel: each theory's group.

## Analysis plan {#sec-s2-analysis}

For H2.1, the correlation between the theory-level mean score and the
theory-level mean completeness rating is estimated within strata, as the
partial correlation given the stratum, by Pearson's $r$ with a Fisher $z$
interval whose standard error is $1/\sqrt{n - `r 3 + n_strata - 1`}$ for $n$
theories, and by a bivariate
mixed model with fixed effects for the strata and crossed random effects for
coders and experts as a check. The correlation within the typical stratum
alone is reported beside it, and the correlation over all theories, which the
known groups widen, is reported as a description.

For H2.2, the theory-level mean scores of the pseudoscientific group are
compared with those of the corroborated and refuted groups by a one-sided
Welch test, and by a mixed model of the encodings with a fixed effect of group
and crossed random intercepts for theories and coders, whose group contrast is
reported with its interval. As sensitivity analyses, the comparison is repeated
without the encodings by coders who recognised the theory and without the
theories that most of their experts knew. The difference between corroborated
and refuted theories is estimated by the same mixed model.

For H2.3, agreement is measured by coefficients that pool the pairs of verdicts
given on each episode, since in the cyclic design two given experts share few
episodes or none, and a kappa for each pair of raters would rest on a handful
of episodes or be undefined. Expert-expert agreement is Fleiss' kappa
[@fleiss1971]: the share of agreeing pairs among the experts of each episode,
averaged over episodes and corrected for chance by the distribution of all
the experts' verdicts. Package-expert agreement is the corresponding
coefficient for the pairs formed by each of the package's verdicts on an
episode (one for each coder's encoding) with each expert's verdict on it,
corrected for chance by the product of the two distributions of verdicts,
which is Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960] computed over all such pairs. The
difference between the two is the estimand. Its interval comes from a
bootstrap that resamples episodes, and experts and coders independently, each
drawn rater entering an episode once (@sec-s1-analysis). The same coefficients
with linear weights, the verdicts ordered from degenerating to progressive, are
reported as a check. The agreement of the package's verdicts across the coders'
encodings of the same episode is reported separately, since it shows how much
the verdict depends on the encoding.

Item-level agreement between each item status (pass against any other status)
and the expert majority answer ('yes' against 'partly' or 'no') is reported by
kappa and Gwet's AC1, with the prevalence of each answer and the raw agreement,
and with bootstrap intervals over theories, for the items that meet the rule of
@sec-s1-measures. 'Cannot tell' is treated as missing for that item and, in a
sensitivity analysis, as 'no'. A theory with fewer than two expert ratings is
left out of the analyses of ratings, and the number left out is reported. The
analyses assume that missing ratings are missing at random given the theory
and the expert.

## Sample size {#sec-s2-size}

For H2.2, the difference of interest is the smallest detectable difference of
the design scenario, `r f(sdd(sem_in[["content"]]), 1)` points: a smaller
average difference between groups would leave most individual theories of the
two groups indistinguishable by their scores. The within-group standard
deviation of a theory's mean score over its encodings is
$\sqrt{\sigma_t^2 + \mathrm{SEM}^2/m}$ with $m$ =
`r design$coders_per_theory`, and the noncentral $t$ distribution gives the
power of the one-sided comparison of one group with the other two taken
together at level `r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)`, the level at which the rule for
C3 applies it (@sec-claims). The widest spread of theories is used, which is
the conservative choice for this comparison.

```{r}
#| label: power-groups
power_groups <- function(n_g, delta, sd_w, alpha) {
  n1 <- n_g; n2 <- 2 * n_g; df <- n1 + n2 - 2
  ncp <- delta / sd_w / sqrt(1 / n1 + 1 / n2)
  1 - pt(qt(1 - alpha / 2, df), df, ncp)
}
sd_within <- function(sd_t, sem) sqrt(sd_t^2 + sem^2 / design$coders_per_theory)
delta_mult <- c(`the SDD` = 1, `half the SDD` = 0.5)
grid_g <- expand.grid(n_g = design$ng_grid, sd_t = c("examples", "pooled"),
                      delta = names(delta_mult), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
grid_g$delta_pts <- delta_mult[grid_g$delta] * sdd(sem_in[["content"]])
grid_g$power <- power_groups(grid_g$n_g, grid_g$delta_pts,
                             sd_within(sd_theory[grid_g$sd_t], sem_in[["content"]]),
                             design$alpha)
need_g <- aggregate(n_g ~ sd_t + delta,
                    data = grid_g[grid_g$power >= design$power, ], FUN = min)
n_group <- need_g$n_g[need_g$sd_t == "pooled" & need_g$delta == "the SDD"]
stopifnot(length(n_group) == 1)
# Two one-sided tests at level alpha, with bounds of plus and minus the
# design SDD, when the true difference between two groups of n_g is zero.
power_tost <- function(n_g, sd_w, bound, alpha) {
  se <- sd_w * sqrt(2 / n_g)
  tc <- qt(1 - alpha, 2 * n_g - 2)
  max(0, pnorm(bound / se - tc) - pnorm(-bound / se + tc))
}
tost <- vapply(c("examples", "pooled"), function(s) {
  power_tost(n_group, sd_within(sd_theory[[s]], sem_in[["content"]]),
             sdd(sem_in[["content"]]), design$alpha)
}, 0)
tost_sentence <- if (tost[["pooled"]] < design$power) {
  paste("Since it falls short of", pct(design$power), "power under the",
        "scenario used to size the groups, the comparison is reported as a",
        "description.")
} else {
  paste("The comparison is nevertheless reported as a description, since no",
        "hypothesis about it is made.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-groups
#| tbl-cap: "Theories needed in each known group for the stated power in H2.2."
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Theory SD` = paste0(need_g$sd_t, " (", f(sd_theory[need_g$sd_t]), ")"),
  Difference = paste0(need_g$delta, " (",
                      f(delta_mult[need_g$delta] * sdd(sem_in[["content"]]), 1),
                      " points)"),
  `Per group` = need_g$n_g, check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

Under the widest spread of theories and a difference equal to the SDD,
`r n_group` theories per group give a power of at least `r pct(design$power)`.
The sample therefore needs at least `r length(known_groups) * n_group` theories
in the known groups and, so that the typical theories are not outnumbered by
any group, at least `r n_group` typical theories. With `r n_group` theories in
each of two groups, a test of equivalence between corroborated and refuted
theories at level `r f(design$alpha, 2)`, with bounds of plus and minus the
design's SDD, would succeed with a probability of `r f(tost[["pooled"]])`
under the widest spread, the scenario used to size the groups, and
`r f(tost[["examples"]])` under the design scenario's spread, when the two
groups do not differ. `r tost_sentence`

For H2.1, the correlation that can be observed is attenuated by the
unreliability of both measures. The reliability of a theory's mean score over
`r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` encodings follows from the ICC of a single
encoding within strata, which is `r f(icc_mid)` in the design scenario and
`r f(icc_of(sd_theory[["pilot"]], sem_in[["content"]]))` and
`r f(icc_of(sd_theory[["pooled"]], sem_in[["content"]]))` under the
pilot's spread and the widest spread. The reliability of the mean of
`r nw(design$experts_per_theory)` expert ratings is computed from an expert ICC
equal to the reviewer reliability and from a higher value of
`r f(design$expert_icc_alt)`. The partial correlation given the
`r nw(n_strata)` strata loses `r nw(n_strata - 1)` degrees of freedom. The
probabilities at the final sample size are given in @sec-final-n.

```{r}
#| label: power-correlation
# Probability that the lower limit of the Fisher z interval exceeds rho0, for
# a partial correlation given q covariates.
power_rho <- function(n, rho, rho0, alpha, q = 0) {
  pnorm((atanh(rho) - atanh(rho0)) * sqrt(n - 3 - q) - qnorm(1 - alpha / 2))
}
```

For H2.3, the agreement of `appraise_amendment()` with experts is simulated in
the planned design: each episode is appraised by
`r nw(design$experts_per_episode)` experts of the pool of
`r design$expert_pool` by the cyclic design, and the package gives one verdict
for each of the `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` encodings. Each episode has a
true verdict drawn with equal probabilities, which is an assumption, since the
distribution of verdicts among published amendments is unknown. Each expert
reproduces it with an accuracy that varies between experts (standard deviation
`r f(design$sd_expert_logit, 1)` on the logit scale) and otherwise picks a
verdict at random, and the package does the same for each coder's encoding
with its own accuracy. The expert accuracy is calibrated so that the expected
expert-expert kappa equals the reviewer kappa (`r f(external$reviewer_kappa)`),
`r f(design$expert_kappa_design)` or `r f(design$expert_kappa_high)`, and the
package's accuracy so that its expected kappa with an expert equals the
expert-expert kappa or falls short of it by `r frac_word(design$c4_margin)`.
Each replicate is analysed with the coefficients of @sec-s2-analysis.

```{r}
#| label: sim-episodes
# Pooled kappa: the share of agreeing pairs within episodes, averaged over
# episodes, corrected for chance. With B = NULL, the pairs are those among the
# columns of A (Fleiss' kappa), and otherwise those between A and B.
pooled_kappa <- function(A, B = NULL, ncat) {
  dist <- function(x) tabulate(x, ncat) / length(x)
  if (is.null(B)) {
    pr <- combn(ncol(A), 2)
    po <- mean(rowMeans(vapply(seq_len(ncol(pr)), function(j)
      A[, pr[1, j]] == A[, pr[2, j]], logical(nrow(A)))))
    pe <- sum(dist(A)^2)
  } else {
    pr <- expand.grid(a = seq_len(ncol(A)), b = seq_len(ncol(B)))
    po <- mean(rowMeans(vapply(seq_len(nrow(pr)), function(j)
      A[, pr$a[j]] == B[, pr$b[j]], logical(nrow(A)))))
    pe <- sum(dist(A) * dist(B))
  }
  (po - pe) / (1 - pe)
}
calibrate_mean_acc <- function(target_mean, sd) {
  uniroot(function(e) sum(GH$w * plogis(e + sd * GH$x)) - target_mean,
          c(-10, 10))$root
}
sim_episodes <- function(n_ep, kap_e, shortfall, reps) {
  share <- design$verdict_share; ncat <- length(share)
  pool <- design$expert_pool; m <- design$experts_per_episode
  k <- design$coders_per_theory
  mean_acc <- sqrt(kap_e)
  eta <- calibrate_mean_acc(mean_acc, design$sd_expert_logit)
  acc_p <- (kap_e - shortfall) / mean_acc
  base <- cyclic(n_ep, m, pool)
  # Verdicts of raters with accuracies acc (episodes by raters).
  rate <- function(acc, truth) {
    ifelse(matrix(runif(length(acc)), n_ep) < acc, truth,
           matrix(sample.int(ncat, length(acc), TRUE, share), n_ep))
  }
  est <- replicate(reps, {
    truth <- sample.int(ncat, n_ep, TRUE, share)
    acc_pool <- plogis(eta + rnorm(pool, 0, design$sd_expert_logit))
    E <- rate(matrix(acc_pool[sample(pool)[base]], n_ep), truth)
    P <- rate(matrix(acc_p, n_ep, k), truth)
    pooled_kappa(P, E, ncat) - pooled_kappa(E, NULL, ncat)
  })
  c(mean = mean(est), sd = sd(est))
}
set.seed(20261127)
kap_levels <- c(external$reviewer_kappa, design$expert_kappa_design,
                design$expert_kappa_high)
grid_e <- expand.grid(n_ep = design$ep_grid, kap_e = kap_levels,
                      shortfall = c("none", "some"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
res_e <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(grid_e)), function(i) {
  g <- grid_e[i, ]
  sim_episodes(g$n_ep, g$kap_e,
               if (g$shortfall == "some") design$c4_margin * g$kap_e else 0,
               design$reps_episode)
}, numeric(2)))
grid_e$mean <- res_e[, "mean"]
grid_e$sd <- res_e[, "sd"]
# Probability that the upper limit lies below zero (H2.3) or that the lower
# limit lies above minus the margin (C4 supported), treating the replication
# standard deviation s as the standard error. For a probability pnorm(r - z)
# with r = (mean + c) / s, the delta method gives the Monte Carlo standard
# error from the replication error of the mean and of s.
p_normal <- function(r, R) {
  list(p = pnorm(r - z_crit),
       mcse = dnorm(r - z_crit) * sqrt(1 / R + r^2 / (2 * (R - 1))))
}
alt <- grid_e[grid_e$shortfall == "some", ]
nul <- grid_e[grid_e$shortfall == "none", ]
h23 <- p_normal(-alt$mean / alt$sd, design$reps_episode)
alt$power <- h23$p
alt$mcse <- h23$mcse
c4 <- p_normal((nul$mean + design$c4_margin * nul$kap_e) / nul$sd,
               design$reps_episode)
alt$p_c4 <- c4$p
alt$mcse_c4 <- c4$mcse
alt$bias_null <- nul$mean
alt$halfwidth_null <- z_crit * nul$sd
ep_ok <- alt$n_ep[alt$kap_e == design$expert_kappa_design &
                    alt$power - 2 * alt$mcse >= design$power]
n_episodes <- if (length(ep_ok)) min(ep_ok) else max(design$ep_grid)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-episodes
#| tbl-cap: "Amendment episodes in the planned design. Power to detect a package-expert agreement that falls short of expert-expert agreement by the margin, and, when there is no shortfall, the mean estimated difference, the half-width of its interval and the probability that C4 is supported. Monte Carlo standard errors are in parentheses."
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Expert-expert kappa` = f(alt$kap_e), Episodes = alt$n_ep,
  Shortfall = f(design$c4_margin * alt$kap_e),
  Power = paste0(f(alt$power), " (", f(alt$mcse, 3), ")"),
  `Mean difference, no shortfall` = f(alt$bias_null, 3),
  `Half-width, no shortfall` = f(alt$halfwidth_null),
  `P(C4 supported), no shortfall` = paste0(f(alt$p_c4), " (",
                                           f(alt$mcse_c4, 3), ")"),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE)
```

If experts agree with each other no better than journal reviewers do, no
feasible number of episodes can show that the package falls short of them, and
the study would instead show that expert appraisal of amendments is too
unreliable to serve as a criterion. With an expert-expert kappa of
`r f(design$expert_kappa_design)`, `r n_episodes` episodes give a power of at
least `r pct(design$power)`, by more than twice its Monte Carlo standard
error, to detect a shortfall of `r frac_word(design$c4_margin)` that value.
When there is no shortfall, the mean estimated difference is within
`r f(max(abs(alt$bias_null[alt$n_ep == n_episodes])), 3)` of zero at that
number of episodes, so the pooled coefficients are not biased by the
incomplete design.

## Inference criteria

C3 is supported if the lower limit of the within-strata correlation exceeds
`r f(design$rho_null)` (H2.1) and the one-sided Welch test finds the
pseudoscientific group's mean score below the others' (H2.2). It is
contradicted if the Holm procedure across two results rejects at least one:
an upper limit of the correlation below `r f(design$rho_null)`, and an upper
limit of the others' mean score minus the pseudoscientific group's below the
design's SDD of `r f(sdd(sem_in[["content"]]), 1)` points, fixed here before
any data are collected, which would mean that the groups differ by less than a
reader could detect. Otherwise C3 is open. C4 is contradicted if H2.3 is
supported, supported if the lower limit of the difference lies above minus
`r frac_word(design$c4_margin)` the expert-expert agreement, and otherwise
open.

## Limitations

The criterion is expert judgement, which is itself fallible, and experts asked
to rate completeness may be swayed by what they know of a theory's standing.
Recording prior knowledge and the rating of empirical standing allows this to be
examined but not removed. Pseudoscientific doctrines are often well known, so
masking may fail for coders and experts alike, and their sources differ in
genre from journal articles. The known groups rest on the record available
now, which may change. Part B gives the experts a summary of Lakatos's
concepts, so it tests whether the rules reproduce what experts conclude with
the same concepts, not whether the concepts are the right ones. Encodings of
episodes record outcomes as of the amended version, while experts may know the
later history of a well-known episode, which the package does not read.
Amendment episodes with both versions in print may over-represent programmes
that survived.

# Study 3: a randomised reader study {#sec-study3}

## Aims and hypotheses

Study 3 measures how often researchers and editors misread
`r nw(design$output_types)` outputs, the checklist score, the gate, the
dossier and the appraisal, whether the wording of version 0.8.0 lowers that
rate relative to the wording of version 0.7.0, and whether the rate under the
0.8.0 wording stays below a stated tolerance. A misreading is endorsing a
statement about an output that the output does not support, for example that a
theory with a higher checklist score is more likely to be true, that a passing
gate shows that the predictions have been tested, that the dossier's test
outcomes were verified by the package or that a progressive verdict shows the
amendment predicted facts not used in building it. Automation bias, the
tendency to over-rely on automation [@goddard2012], occurs in naive and expert
users alike and is not prevented by training or instructions
[@parasuraman2010], although a systematic review lists training, emphasis on
users' accountability and design factors such as the position of advice on the
screen among the reported mitigators [@goddard2012]. Changing the wording of a
display may therefore reduce misreading, though by how much is uncertain.

- H3.1: the probability of endorsing a misreading is lower in the 0.8.0 wording
  than in the 0.7.0 wording.
- H3.2: in the 0.8.0 wording, the rate at which participants endorse the
  misreadings of each output is below `r pct(design$misread_tolerance)`, a
  tolerance that is our value judgement.
- H3.3: the 0.8.0 wording does not lower the odds of endorsing correct readings
  by as much as an odds ratio of `r f(design$ni_margin_or)`, so that a lower
  misreading rate does not come from readers rejecting every statement. The
  margin equals the design effect of H3.1: a wording that lowered correct
  readings as much as it is meant to lower misreadings would be making readers
  reject statements in general.

Claim C5 concerns what readers of the 0.8.0 wording conclude, so it is decided
by H3.2 alone. H3.1 answers the comparative question of whether the 0.8.0
wording is read better than the 0.7.0 wording.

## Design

Study 3 is a two-arm parallel randomised experiment. Participants are
randomised to the 0.7.0 or the 0.8.0 wording, stratified by role (researcher or
editor), in permuted blocks generated by a script whose seed is held by someone
outside the study team. Each participant sees the score, the gate and the
dossier for `r nw(design$theories_per_reader)` example theories and the
appraisal of one amendment, and judges
`r design$misread_items + design$correct_items` statements in a random order:
for each of the `r nw(design$output_types)` outputs,
`r nw(design$misread_per_type)` that state misreadings and
`r nw(design$correct_per_type)` that state correct readings. Statements are
crossed with the wording conditions, and participants are nested in them.

## Materials

The outputs are produced by the releases tagged v0.7.0 and v0.8.0, each
identified by its commit, from the package's shipped example theories: the
app's checklist card and result text, the gate's explanation and the dossier
for two theories, and the appraisal of the panic-network amendment, the only
amendment pair the package ships. The two releases can compute different
values from the same file, since 0.8.0 reads some items differently, and
showing each release's own values would confound the wording with the values.
The values shown, the score, the item statuses, the gate's outcome and the
appraisal's verdict, are therefore those computed by the 0.8.0 release in both
arms, inserted into each release's own templates, so that the arms differ in
wording and in what each release displays and not in the values. The
statements are written by the study team and reviewed by two people outside it
for whether each is unambiguously supported or unsupported by both versions of
the output. A statement that either reviewer judges ambiguous is rewritten or
dropped before registration. The statements are piloted for comprehension with
readers who do not take part in the main study.
`r Nw(design$attention_items)` instructed-response items check attention.

## Participants and recruitment

Researchers are people who hold or are studying for a doctorate in a
behavioural or social science, recruited through mailing lists of learned
societies, departmental lists and social media. Editors are people who serve or
have served as editors or associate editors of journals in those fields,
invited individually from public listings of editorial boards. Editors are
sought until they make up `r pct(design$editor_share)` of the sample or
recruitment closes. Participants receive a voucher for their time. People who
have used theoryforge, or who took part in Studies 1 and 2, are excluded.

## Procedure

The study runs online. After consent, participants answer questions about their
role, field and experience with preregistration and theory appraisal, read the
outputs of the first theory, judge its statements as 'supported by what is
shown' or 'not supported by what is shown' and rate their confidence, and then
do the same for the second theory and for the amendment. The outputs stay
visible while they answer. Participants are told that they are helping to
evaluate how a research tool's outputs are read. They are not told that two
wordings are compared until the debriefing, which explains the comparison and
shows both versions.

## Measures

The primary outcome is, for each participant and misreading statement, whether
the participant endorsed the misreading. Secondary outcomes are the endorsement
of correct statements, the misreading rate for each output, confidence and
time spent.

## Analysis plan

The primary model is a logistic mixed model of endorsement on the misreading
statements with fixed effects of wording and role and random effects for
participants and for statements, with a random slope of wording over
statements, as the design justifies [@barr2013]. The odds ratio for wording is
reported with its Wald and profile likelihood intervals, and the marginal
difference in misreading rates with an interval from a parametric bootstrap of
the model. For H3.2, the misreading rate of each output in the 0.8.0 arm is the
average over its registered misreading statements of the probability of
endorsing each, estimated by a logistic mixed model of that arm with fixed
effects for the statements and random intercepts for participants, with an
interval from a parametric bootstrap. The statements are treated as fixed
here, because the tolerance concerns the registered misreadings themselves,
and as random in H3.1, whose question is whether the wording effect holds for
misreadings in general. H3.3 uses the model of H3.1 on the correct statements
and is tested against the margin by a one-sided test [@lakens2017].
Interactions of wording with role and with output type are exploratory.
Participants who fail every attention item are excluded, and a sensitivity
analysis includes them. Unanswered statements are treated as missing at random
given the participant and the statement, which the mixed models accommodate.

## Sample size {#sec-s3-size}

The power for H3.1 is first computed from an approximation and then checked by
simulating and fitting the planned model. In the approximation, with the arms
coded $x = \pm\tfrac{1}{2}$, $n$ participants per arm and $I$ misreading
statements, the variance of the estimated log odds ratio is

$$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta) \approx \frac{2\sigma_u^2}{n} +
\frac{\sigma_v^2}{I} + \frac{2}{nI\,\bar w},$$

where $\sigma_u$ is the participant standard deviation, $\sigma_v$ the standard
deviation of the wording effect over statements and $\bar w$ the mean of
$p(1-p)$ over participants and statements. The middle term does not shrink as
participants are added, so with a fixed set of statements the power does not
approach one as the number of participants grows [@westfall2014]. The baseline
probability of a misreading under the 0.7.0 wording, for a typical participant
and statement, is taken as `r f(p_hoekstra)`, from the finding of
@hoekstra2014 that researchers and students endorsed, on average, more than
`r nw(external$false_endorsed)` of `r nw(external$false_items)` false
statements about a confidence interval, and as `r f(design$p0_low)` as a lower
alternative. The design effect is an odds ratio of `r f(design$or_design)`,
which at a baseline of `r f(p_hoekstra)` lowers the misreading probability to
`r f(plogis(qlogis(p_hoekstra) + log(design$or_design)))`, with
`r f(design$or_large)` as a larger alternative.

```{r}
#| label: power-reader
w_bar <- function(mu, sd) {
  p <- plogis(mu + sd * GH$x)
  sum(GH$w * p * (1 - p))
}
# Power of the one-sided test of the wording coefficient: for H3.1 that it is
# below zero, and with a margin that it lies above log(margin) (H3.3).
power_reader <- function(n, p0, or, I = design$misread_items, margin = NULL) {
  b1 <- log(or)
  w <- w_bar(qlogis(p0) + b1 / 2, sqrt(design$sd_reader^2 + design$sd_item^2))
  v <- 2 * design$sd_reader^2 / n + design$sd_item_slope^2 / I +
    2 / (n * I * w)
  if (is.null(margin)) pnorm(-b1 / sqrt(v) - z_crit) else
    pnorm((b1 - log(margin)) / sqrt(v) - z_crit)
}
grid_r <- expand.grid(n = design$arm_grid, p0 = c(design$p0_low, p_hoekstra),
                      or = c(design$or_large, design$or_design))
grid_r$power <- mapply(power_reader, grid_r$n, grid_r$p0, grid_r$or)
design_rows <- grid_r$p0 == p_hoekstra & grid_r$or == design$or_design
arm_ok <- grid_r$n[design_rows & grid_r$power >= design$power]
n_arm_cf <- if (length(arm_ok)) min(arm_ok) else max(design$arm_grid)
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-reader
sim_reader <- function(n, p0, or, reps, I = design$misread_items,
                       margin = NULL) {
  d <- expand.grid(item = factor(seq_len(I)), pid = factor(seq_len(2 * n)))
  d$x <- ifelse(as.integer(d$pid) <= n, -0.5, 0.5)
  gen <- function() {
    u <- rnorm(2 * n, 0, design$sd_reader)
    w <- rnorm(I, 0, design$sd_item)
    v <- rnorm(I, 0, design$sd_item_slope)
    eta <- qlogis(p0) + log(or) / 2 + log(or) * d$x + u[d$pid] + w[d$item] +
      v[d$item] * d$x
    rbinom(nrow(d), 1, plogis(eta))
  }
  # The template fit gives the starting values of every refit, so it is drawn
  # again (up to 20 times) while it lies on the boundary.
  for (attempt in 1:20) {
    d$y <- gen()
    fit <- glmer(y ~ x + (1 | pid) + (1 + x | item), data = d,
                 family = binomial, nAGQ = 0, control = glmerControl(
                   check.conv.singular = .makeCC(action = "ignore", tol = 1e-4)))
    if (!isSingular(fit, tol = 1e-4)) break
  }
  z <- t(replicate(reps, {
    warned <- FALSE
    f_r <- withCallingHandlers(refit(fit, gen()), warning = function(w) {
      warned <<- TRUE
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    })
    s <- summary(f_r)$coefficients
    c(est = s["x", "Estimate"], se = s["x", "Std. Error"], warned = warned,
      singular = isSingular(f_r, tol = 1e-4))
  }))
  hit <- if (is.null(margin)) z[, "est"] / z[, "se"] < -z_crit else
    (z[, "est"] - log(margin)) / z[, "se"] > z_crit
  p <- mean(hit)
  c(power = p, mcse = mcse_p(p, reps), warned = sum(z[, "warned"]),
    singular = sum(z[, "singular"]))
}
set.seed(20261128)
n_arm <- n_arm_cf
step <- diff(design$arm_grid)[1]
repeat {
  sim_r <- sim_reader(n_arm, p_hoekstra, design$or_design, design$reps_reader)
  if (sim_r[["power"]] >= design$power || n_arm >= max(design$arm_grid)) break
  n_arm <- n_arm + step
}
fit_sentence <- function(s) {
  count <- function(k) if (k == 0) "none" else nw(k)
  paste0("Of these fits, ", count(s[["warned"]]),
         " raised a convergence warning and ", count(s[["singular"]]),
         " ended singular. All were kept.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reader
#| tbl-cap: "Approximate power for H3.1 by participants per arm, baseline misreading probability and odds ratio."
show_n <- design$arm_grid[seq(1, length(design$arm_grid), by = 2)]
tab_r <- reshape(grid_r[grid_r$n %in% show_n, ], idvar = c("p0", "or"),
                 timevar = "n", direction = "wide")
names(tab_r) <- c("Baseline", "Odds ratio", paste(show_n, "per arm"))
tab_r[, -(1:2)] <- lapply(tab_r[, -(1:2)], f)
tab_r$Baseline <- f(tab_r$Baseline)
tab_r$`Odds ratio` <- f(tab_r$`Odds ratio`)
knitr::kable(tab_r, row.names = FALSE)
```

The approximation reaches a power of `r pct(design$power)` in the design
scenario with `r n_arm_cf` participants per arm. Fitting the planned model to
`r design$reps_reader` simulated data sets with `r n_arm` participants per arm
gave a power of `r f(sim_r[["power"]])` (Monte Carlo standard error
`r f(sim_r[["mcse"]], 3)`). `r fit_sentence(sim_r)` The planned sample is
`r n_arm` per arm, `r 2 * n_arm` in all. The simulation uses the fast
approximation of the likelihood that lme4 offers (`nAGQ = 0`), while the
analysis will use the Laplace approximation. The decision rests on the
simulation, because the closed form summarises the spread of statement
difficulties by one mean and can misstate the power. Recruitment closes when
`r 2 * n_arm` participants have completed the study or when the recruitment
period in @sec-timeline ends, whichever comes first, and a shortfall is
reported with the power it implies.

```{r}
#| label: power-h33
# H3.3: no true effect on correct readings, tested against the margin.
h33_cf <- vapply(c(design = design$p_correct, alt = design$p_correct_alt),
                 function(p) power_reader(n_arm, p, 1, design$correct_items,
                                          design$ni_margin_or), 0)
h33_half <- power_reader(n_arm, design$p_correct, 1, design$correct_items / 2,
                         design$ni_margin_or)
set.seed(20261131)
sim_h33 <- sim_reader(n_arm, design$p_correct, 1, design$reps_reader,
                      I = design$correct_items, margin = design$ni_margin_or)
```

For H3.3, the probability that a typical participant endorses a correct
statement under the 0.7.0 wording is taken as `r f(design$p_correct)`, an
assumption, with `r f(design$p_correct_alt)` as an alternative under which the
correct statements carry less information. When the wording has no effect on
correct readings, the approximation gives a power of
`r f(h33_cf[["design"]])` with `r n_arm` participants per arm and
`r design$correct_items` correct statements (`r f(h33_cf[["alt"]])` under the
alternative), and fitting the planned model to `r design$reps_reader`
simulated data sets gave `r f(sim_h33[["power"]])` (Monte Carlo standard error
`r f(sim_h33[["mcse"]], 3)`). `r fit_sentence(sim_h33)` The number of correct
statements matters because of the middle term of the variance: with half as
many, the approximate power would be `r f(h33_half)`.

```{r}
#| label: power-rates
# H3.2: standard error of an output's misreading rate in the 0.8.0 arm, the
# mean over its J registered statements, treated as fixed and placed at the
# normal quantiles of the statement distribution, with n participants.
rate_se <- function(n, p, J) {
  w <- qnorm((seq_len(J) - 0.5) / J) * design$sd_item
  pj_of <- function(mu) {
    vapply(w, function(wj) plogis(mu + wj + design$sd_reader * GH$x),
           numeric(length(GH$x)))
  }
  mu <- uniroot(function(m) sum(GH$w * rowMeans(pj_of(m))) - p, c(-12, 12))$root
  pj <- pj_of(mu)
  mbar <- rowMeans(pj)
  v_within <- rowSums(pj * (1 - pj)) / J^2
  sqrt((sum(GH$w * (mbar - p)^2) + sum(GH$w * v_within)) / n)
}
p_design_08 <- sum(GH$w * plogis(qlogis(p_hoekstra) + log(design$or_design) +
                   sqrt(design$sd_reader^2 + design$sd_item^2) * GH$x))
z_holm4 <- qnorm(1 - design$alpha / 2 / design$output_types)
rates <- data.frame(p = sort(c(design$rate_grid, p_design_08)))
rates$se <- vapply(rates$p, function(p)
  rate_se(n_arm, p, design$misread_per_type), 0)
rates$support <- pnorm((design$misread_tolerance - rates$p) / rates$se - z_crit)
rates$contradict <- pnorm((rates$p - design$misread_tolerance) / rates$se -
                          z_holm4)
# A rate of half the tolerance and one of one and a half times it.
p_low <- design$misread_tolerance / 2
p_high <- 1.5 * design$misread_tolerance
se_low <- rate_se(n_arm, p_low, design$misread_per_type)
se_high <- rate_se(n_arm, p_high, design$misread_per_type)
oc_low <- pnorm((design$misread_tolerance - p_low) / se_low - z_crit)
oc_high <- pnorm((p_high - design$misread_tolerance) / se_high - z_holm4)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rates
#| tbl-cap: "H3.2 for one output: approximate standard error of its misreading rate in the 0.8.0 arm, probability that the upper limit lies below the tolerance (the output meets C5's condition) and probability that the lower limit lies above it at the most stringent Holm threshold (C5 contradicted by this output), by true rate."
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `True rate` = f(rates$p), `Standard error` = f(rates$se, 3),
  `P(below tolerance)` = f(rates$support),
  `P(above tolerance)` = f(rates$contradict), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE)
```

For H3.2, @tbl-rates gives the operating characteristics for one output, with
`r nw(design$misread_per_type)` misreading statements and `r n_arm`
participants in the 0.8.0 arm. A true rate of half the tolerance,
`r f(p_low)`, is shown to lie below it with a probability of `r f(oc_low)`,
and a rate of one and a half times the tolerance, `r f(p_high)`, to lie above
it with a probability of `r f(oc_high)`. Under the
design scenario of H3.1, the rate in the 0.8.0 arm would be about
`r f(p_design_08)`, far above the tolerance, so the design scenario expects C5
to be contradicted. C5 needs every output to meet its condition, so the
probability of supporting it is lower than for any one output.

## Inference criteria

H3.1 is tested by the one-sided Wald test of the wording coefficient at level
`r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)`. Its result says whether the 0.8.0 wording lowers
misreading and does not decide C5. C5 is supported if, for each of the
`r nw(design$output_types)` outputs, the upper limit of the 0.8.0 arm's
misreading rate lies below `r pct(design$misread_tolerance)` (H3.2),
contradicted if the Holm procedure across the outputs finds the rate above
`r pct(design$misread_tolerance)` for at least one, and otherwise open. H3.3 is
tested one-sided at level `r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)` against the margin.

## Limitations

The study measures reading in an online task with the outputs in view, which
is not how outputs are read in a review or in a decision about a grant, and the
statements are a sample of possible misreadings written by the study team. The
rates of H3.2 refer to the registered statements, and other misreadings may be
more or less common. Participants who volunteer may be more careful readers
than average. The appraisal is shown for one amendment only, the one the
package ships. The comparison concerns two wordings of the same values, so it
cannot show whether a display that leads with item statuses and leaves out the
aggregate would be read better, which is a question for a later study.

# Predictive validity: a later cliometric study {#sec-cliometric}

The studies above relate the package's outputs to encodings, experts and
readers at one time. Whether the checklist profile, or the record of amendments,
carries information about the later fate of theories is a question of
predictive validity. @meehl2002 argued that the history of science shows
scientists appraising theories by attributes such as parsimony, the number,
qualitative diversity, novelty and numerical precision of the facts derived and
the number of facts misderived, and that a statistical composite of such
attributes could give an actuarial basis for theory appraisal, which he called
cliometric metatheory. Faust and Meehl [-@faust1992; -@faust2002] proposed
studying the historical track record of scientific episodes and judgements by
the methods of empirical science. A cliometric study of theoryforge would apply
that proposal to the package's outputs.

In outline, a sample of theories with dated versions is drawn from the
historical record of a defined field. Each version is encoded from the sources
available at its date, by coders who follow the written protocol and are kept
as far as possible from the theory's later history: names and dates are
masked, sources are limited to those available at the date, and recognition is
recorded. The outputs at each date, including the item statuses, the revised
profile, the attributes in Meehl's list that a file can record and the
appraisals of successive amendments, are computed by a registered script and
archived before any outcome is known to the analyst. Separately, historians or
domain experts who do not see the encodings classify the fate of each theory a
fixed number of years after the version's date, by registered criteria
(retained and corroborated, retained after amendment, absorbed into another
theory, abandoned). The registered analysis then asks whether a prespecified
composite, fixed before the outcomes are joined, predicts fate better than
simple baselines, such as the theory's age, the number of studies citing it at
the date and prediction from the base rates alone, by discrimination and
calibration under cross-validation, with versions nested in theories. A
prospective variant would register theories encoded now and follow them.

The study is not powered here. Its size depends on how many theories have dated
versions and recorded fates, which a scoping review must establish first, and
on base rates of abandonment that are unknown. Its main threats are already
clear: survivorship in the historical record, hindsight entering the encoding
however carefully coders are kept from it, fates that are themselves contested
and the possibility that any association reflects a field's fashions rather than
the theories.

# Final sample sizes and workload {#sec-final-n}

```{r}
#| label: final-n
by_groups <- n_strata * n_group > n_study1
n_sentence <- if (by_groups) {
  paste0("The number of theories is set by H2.2. Study 1 alone would need ",
         n_study1, ", and the larger sample gives more precision elsewhere, ",
         "though less than its size suggests.")
} else {
  "The number of theories is set by Study 1."
}
n_theories <- round_up(max(n_study1, n_strata * n_group), nrow(sts9))
n_typical <- n_theories - length(known_groups) * n_group
files_theory <- n_theories * design$coders_per_theory
files_episode <- n_episodes * 2 * design$coders_per_theory
coder_hours <- (files_theory + files_episode) * design$hours_per_file
expert_ratings <- n_theories * design$experts_per_theory
expert_appraisals <- n_episodes * design$experts_per_episode
expert_hours <- expert_ratings * design$hours_per_rating[["theory"]] +
  expert_appraisals * design$hours_per_rating[["episode"]]
agent_files <- (n_theories + 2 * n_episodes) * design$agent_runs
# Expert load in the cyclic designs.
load_th <- range(table(cyclic(n_theories, design$experts_per_theory,
                              design$expert_pool)))
load_ep <- range(table(cyclic(n_episodes, design$experts_per_episode,
                              design$expert_pool)))
apart_th <- pairs_apart(cyclic(n_theories, design$experts_per_theory,
                               design$expert_pool), design$expert_pool)
apart_ep <- pairs_apart(cyclic(n_episodes, design$experts_per_episode,
                               design$expert_pool), design$expert_pool)
range_text <- function(r) {
  if (r[1] == r[2]) r[1] else paste(r[1], if (r[2] - r[1] == 1) "or" else "to",
                                    r[2])
}
# H2.1 at the final number of theories, under each spread of theories.
h21 <- expand.grid(rho = design$rho_true,
                   icc_e = c(external$reviewer_icc, design$expert_icc_alt),
                   spread = names(sd_theory), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
h21$rel_score <- sb(icc_of(sd_theory[h21$spread], sem_in[["content"]]),
                    design$coders_per_theory)
h21$rho_obs <- h21$rho * sqrt(h21$rel_score *
                                sb(h21$icc_e, design$experts_per_theory))
h21$positive <- power_rho(n_theories, h21$rho_obs, 0, design$alpha,
                          n_strata - 1)
h21$support <- power_rho(n_theories, h21$rho_obs, design$rho_null,
                         design$alpha, n_strata - 1)
# H1.4 at the largest grid value not above the final number of theories.
n_h14 <- max(design$n_grid[design$n_grid <= n_theories])
h14_rows <- grid_s$n == n_h14 & grid_s$sem == "content"
h14 <- setNames(grid_s$p_half[h14_rows], grid_s$sd_t[h14_rows])
# Per-item agreement on a pass or not-pass status, one unit per theory, at the
# pass share of the item that varied in the pilot and at a skewed share.
set.seed(20261129)
item_pass <- c(pilot = unname(pilot$item_pass_share[varying_items[1]]),
               skewed = 0.9)
item_hw <- vapply(item_pass, function(pass) {
  z_crit * sim_alpha(n_theories, 1, c(pass, 1 - pass), pilot$kappa_element,
                     min(design$sd_theory_logit), design$sd_coder_logit, sts9,
                     design$reps_alpha)[["sd"]]
}, numeric(1))
```

The planned sample for Studies 1 and 2 is `r n_theories` theories:
`r n_group` in each of the `r nw(length(known_groups))` known groups and
`r n_typical` typical theories from the two sampling frames, each encoded by
`r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` human coders and run
`r nw(design$agent_runs)` times by the agent, and `r n_episodes` amendment
episodes, each encoded as a prior and an amended file by
`r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` coders. The coders write
`r f(files_theory + files_episode, 0)` files, which at
`r f(design$hours_per_file[["low"]], 0)` to
`r f(design$hours_per_file[["high"]], 0)` hours a file
(`r f(design$hours_per_file[["mid"]], 0)` in the middle estimate) is
`r f(coder_hours[["mid"]], 0)` hours, or
`r f((files_theory + files_episode) / design$coder_pool, 0)` files and
`r f(coder_hours[["mid"]] / design$coder_pool, 0)` hours for each of the
`r nw(design$coder_pool)` coders
(`r f(coder_hours[["low"]] / design$coder_pool, 0)` to
`r f(coder_hours[["high"]] / design$coder_pool, 0)`). The experts give
`r expert_ratings` theory ratings and `r expert_appraisals` episode
appraisals: in the cyclic designs, each expert rates
`r range_text(load_th)` theories and appraises `r range_text(load_ep)`
episodes, about `r f(expert_hours / design$expert_pool, 0)` hours for each of
`r design$expert_pool` experts. Of the pairs of experts, `r pct(apart_th)`
share no theory and `r pct(apart_ep)` no episode, which is why expert
agreement is measured by coefficients that pool pairs within units. The agent
writes `r agent_files` files. If the funds available cannot pay for these
hours, the number of theories will be reduced before registration and the
precision recomputed with this document's code.

`r n_sentence`
@tbl-h21 gives, for H2.1, the correlation that can be observed once the
unreliability of the score (averaged over `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)`
encodings) and of the experts' mean rating is taken into account, under each
spread of theories, with the probability that the lower limit exceeds zero and
the probability that it exceeds `r f(design$rho_null)`, which H2.1 and claim
C3 need. Under the design scenario's spread, the probability of supporting H2.1
is at most `r f(max(h21$support[h21$spread == "examples"]))`, even with a high
true correlation and experts who agree well. It is at most
`r f(max(h21$support[h21$spread == "pilot"]))` if typical theories differ as
little as the pilot's, and reaches
`r f(max(h21$support[h21$spread == "pooled"]))` only under the widest spread.
For H1.4, the approximate probability of supporting C2 at `r n_h14` theories is
`r f(h14[["examples"]])` under the design scenario, whose true ICC is
`r f(icc_mid)`, `r f(h14[["pilot"]])` under the pilot's spread and
`r f(h14[["pooled"]])` under the widest spread. Whether C2 and C3 can be
supported thus depends on how much typical theories differ, which the study
will estimate. Agreement on a single checklist item, with one unit per theory,
is estimated with a half-width of about `r f(item_hw[["pilot"]])` when
`r pct(item_pass[["pilot"]])` of the files pass the item, as for
'`r varying_items[1]`' in the pilot, and `r f(item_hw[["skewed"]])` when
`r pct(item_pass[["skewed"]])` do, so item-level results are descriptive.
Study 3 needs `r 2 * n_arm` participants.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-h21
#| tbl-cap: "H2.1 at the final number of theories, by spread of theories: reliability of the mean score, observable correlation, probability that the lower interval limit exceeds zero and probability that it exceeds the level H2.1 and claim C3 need."
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Spread = paste0(h21$spread, " (", f(sd_theory[h21$spread]), ")"),
  `True correlation` = f(h21$rho), `Expert ICC` = f(h21$icc_e),
  `Score reliability` = f(h21$rel_score),
  `Observable correlation` = f(h21$rho_obs),
  `P(lower limit above zero)` = f(h21$positive),
  `P(lower limit above level)` = f(h21$support), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE)
```

# Data management {#sec-data}

The data are the segmented source passages, the theory files and statement
codes written by coders and agents, the package's outputs, the classification
panel's assignments, the expert item answers, ratings and appraisals, and the
reader study's responses. During collection, they are held on storage managed
by the University of Oxford, with access limited to the study team.
Participants are identified by codes, and the key linking codes to names and
contact details is held separately, used only to pay participants and to send
the debriefing, and deleted once those are complete and no later than
`r nw(design$withdraw_months)` month after the end of data collection for the
study concerned. Theory files, statement codes, outputs, ratings and responses
are stored in open formats (YAML, CSV and JSON) with a codebook. Personal data
are processed under UK data protection law and the University's policies, and
kept for the period those policies set.

When the results are reported, anonymised data are deposited, under a licence
that allows reuse with attribution, in a public repository with a persistent
identifier. Anonymisation follows the deletion of the key: free-text answers
are screened for identifying details, and variables that could identify a
person in combination, such as an editor's role, field and experience, are
coarsened or withheld until every combination describes at least
`r nw(design$min_cell)` participants. Participants consent to this deposit when
they agree to take part. Source passages under copyright are not deposited, but
their bibliographic details and page ranges are.

# Ethics {#sec-ethics}

Each study will be submitted for review under the University of Oxford's
research ethics process, overseen by its Central University Research Ethics
Committee, through the research ethics committee responsible for the
investigator's department, and no participant will be recruited, nor any
statement piloted with readers, before approval. The approval references will
be added to each registration when they are issued. All participants give
informed consent, including consent to the deposit of their anonymised data,
and may withdraw without giving a reason until the key linking their code to
their name is deleted, on a date stated in the participant information. The
studies carry minimal risk. Coders' agreement is a property of the procedure
under study and not an assessment of the coders, and no result will be reported
for a named coder or expert. Editors' responses are not linked to their
journals. Study 3 does not tell participants before they take part that two
wordings are compared, because knowing it would change how they read, and the
debriefing explains the comparison and offers withdrawal. The investigator's
interest as the package's maintainer is declared in the application and in
every report.

# Open materials and registration {#sec-open}

The following are made public at registration of the study concerned.

- This protocol and its code.
- The written encoding protocol and the training materials.
- The search strings and the eligibility and classification criteria.
- The expert instrument and the one-page summary of Lakatos's concepts.
- The reader-study materials, statements and randomisation script.
- The agent's instructions and model identifier.
- The package releases used, by commit.
- The analysis scripts, run first on simulated data of the registered shape.

The screening decisions, the list of sampled theories and episodes with their
sources and page ranges, and the panel's assignments are made public before
encoding begins. The coordinator's archived answers and the data described in
@sec-data are made public when the results are reported.

```{r}
           "Piloting of the Study 3 statements with readers",

           "Study 3 analysis and report",
           "Encoding protocol, search strings, criteria and expert instrument",
           "Ethics review of Studies 1 and 2",
           "Registration of Studies 1 and 2",
           "Searches, screening and classification panel",
           "Coder recruitment and training",
           "Study 1 encoding of theories, and agent runs",
           "Study 2 expert ratings of theories",
           "Encoding and expert appraisal of amendment episodes",
           "Analysis of Studies 1 and 2 by the registered scripts",
           "Reports and deposit of data"),
  start = c(1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 1, 4, 6, 7, 7, 10, 11, 12, 19, 21),
  end = c(3, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 4, 5, 6, 9, 9, 17, 18, 19, 21, 23))
at <- function(task) timeline[timeline$Task == task, ]
before <- function(a, b) at(a)$end < at(b)$start
stopifnot(all(timeline$end >= timeline$start),
          before("Ethics review of Study 3",
                 "Piloting of the Study 3 statements with readers"),
          before("Piloting of the Study 3 statements with readers",
                 "Registration of Study 3"),
          before("Registration of Study 3", "Study 3 data collection"),
          before("Encoding protocol, search strings, criteria and expert instrument",
                 "Registration of Studies 1 and 2"),
          before("Ethics review of Studies 1 and 2",
                 "Registration of Studies 1 and 2"),
          before("Registration of Studies 1 and 2",
                 "Searches, screening and classification panel"),
          before("Registration of Studies 1 and 2",
                 "Coder recruitment and training"),
          before("Searches, screening and classification panel",
                 "Study 1 encoding of theories, and agent runs"),
          before("Coder recruitment and training",
                 "Study 1 encoding of theories, and agent runs"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Task = timeline$Task,
                        Months = ifelse(timeline$start == timeline$end,
                                        timeline$start,
                                        paste(timeline$start, "to",
                                              timeline$end))),
             row.names = FALSE)
```

Ethics approval precedes any recruitment and the piloting of statements with
readers, and each registration follows the completion of the materials it
fixes and precedes the searches and data collection it governs. The programme
takes `r max(timeline$end)` months, and Study 3 can be reported by month
`r at("Study 3 analysis and report")$end`.
